edition.article:
There is a strange gap at the center of musculoskeletal medicine. The founding essay reports what it says anyone with a foam roller can check: [small, discrete, exquisitely tender points in muscle and fascia]{claim=VASO-C001} — dozens per body, densest at the hips and shoulders, more with each passing decade. That is the essay’s report, and it matches widespread practitioner lore; how common such points are across the population has never been measured. The one population record this ledger holds is a 1994 general-practice survey in which two people who reported no pain at all had eleven or more examiner-elicited tender points at fixed sites — a pain-selected sample from which no prevalence figure follows, discussed below. Roll across a point, the essay says, and it announces itself. Yet open the research literature and you find scientists arguing about what these points are — and, in part, [about whether the “trigger point” is a real, reliably identifiable thing at all]{claim=VASO-C030}.

This case examines a chain of ideas offered to close that gap, and the accounts that compete with it. The chain runs from textbook smooth-muscle physiology, through a minority hypothesis about blood and computation, to Tibetan and Indian contemplative anatomy, and arrives at a proposal with a slogan: a knot is a *state*, not a *scar* — something the body is actively doing and could stop doing, rather than tissue that has been damaged. The lower rungs of the chain are established science. The upper rungs have never been tested. And three pictures of what the state might be are on the table:

- **The latched arteriole.** A small vessel inside the muscle, held shut by smooth muscle in its low-energy “latch,” starving a small territory; the electrical activity, the acid and the guarding are downstream.
- **The stuck perforator.** A vessel-and-nerve bundle where it pierces the fascia under the skin, held by ordinary sympathetic tone, a collar of gelled hyaluronan and a fascial tether — no latch required.
- **Guarding, densification and interpretation.** Ordinary neuromuscular guarding in skeletal muscle, possibly with thickened fascial lubricant, and a felt release supplied by expectation riding on global relaxation.

All three say a knot is a state rather than a scar. They disagree about which state, in which tissue, held by what — and about whether the breath is a key at all.

## A phenomenon without a mechanism

Part of the reason the fight has run so long is structural. Medicine is organized by organ system: orthopedics owns bones, neurology owns nerves, cardiology owns the pipes. Nobody owns muscle tone — the continuous, neurally set background contraction of soft tissue — so there are no billing codes, no imaging protocols, no funding lines. The skeptics’ line, “there is no evidence,” is partly circular: there is little evidence in part because nobody has been paid to look.

But the skeptical case deserves its full weight. A systematic review of examination-reliability studies (Lucas and colleagues, 2009) concluded that manual examination for trigger points has not been shown to be reliable or valid — partly because no accepted reference standard exists for what one is — and could not be recommended as an objective diagnostic test. The most pointed peer-reviewed critique (Quintner, Bove and Cohen, 2015) argues that the construct rests on circular reasoning: the lesion has never been demonstrated, examiners disagree, and the clinical phenomena can be explained otherwise. That critique drew a rebuttal, and the exchange rather than either paper is the state of the debate. The construct’s defenders concede the core of the complaint. The NIH-affiliated imaging group whose work appears below writes that examination results “can vary depending on the clinician’s training and experience,” and a Polish sports-medicine group that in 2025 imaged trigger points in the calves of runners states that “there is no gold standard technique for detecting them,” that manual palpation “has significant inter-observer variability that cannot be meaningfully improved after training,” and that this is why they added ultrasound to the examiner’s thumb — which confirmed 71.5 percent of the hard spots the examiner had palpated and attributed the rest to tendinous cores and musculotendinous junctions. The dispute, then, reaches the observation base: a quarter of what feels like a knot may be something else, and what remains is located by a method no one has shown to be reproducible. That is one reason this case grades the first claim above as only *weakly* supported; the other is that its second half — that the points are common across the general population — has never been measured, and is held here on the essay’s report and a second-hand clinic estimate.

What population data exist are thin. The only prevalence figure the ledger holds is a 1986 clinic-based estimate, quoted second-hand in a 2011 introduction, that myofascial pain affects some 23 million Americans — a figure for a pain syndrome, not a count of tender points in ordinary people. One community survey using rheumatology’s eighteen-site tender-point protocol is in the ledger: Croft, Schollum and Silman examined 177 adults drawn from two general practices in north-west England in 1994. The examined sample had been selected on reported pain, so the survey cannot say how universal tender points are — but two of the people who reported no pain at all had eleven or more tender points, the threshold rheumatology used to diagnose fibromyalgia, and most of those with chronic widespread pain had fewer than eleven. Examiner-elicited tenderness, at fixed sites, in people with nothing to complain of: that is the nearest instrumented cousin the ledger has of what the roller reports — two individuals, in a sample chosen for pain, from which nothing about prevalence follows. The founding essay’s further statements — medians of six tender points in women and three in men, counts tracking distress and poor sleep — are held here on the essay’s word alone; the survey’s own figures on those points have not entered as records.

What survives the critique is a set of instrumented findings, and they cut both ways. Shah and colleagues (2008) sampled the fluid at active trigger points and found [it more acidic and loaded with mediators of pain and inflammation — bradykinin, substance P, CGRP]{claim=VASO-C005}. The study had about nine volunteers and, as its title says, the mediators were elevated at sites remote from the points as well as near them. Something is there, and it is chemically angry — but whether what is there is *local* is less settled than it sounds.

The most detailed look comes from the same NIH lineage. In 2011 Ballyns, Shah and colleagues imaged the upper trapezius of forty-four patients with acute neck pain, 169 sites in all, with the sonographers blinded to which sites the examiner had called active (painful on its own), latent (painful only when pressed) or normal. Vibration sonoelastography — shaking the tissue with a handheld massager and mapping where it fails to move — found a graded region of stiffness: [about 0.57 square centimeters at active points against 0.36 at latent points]{claim=VASO-C182}, and [0.17 square centimeters at palpably normal sites]{claim=VASO-C187}, with both classes of point significantly larger than normal tissue. Area alone sorted the three site classes on receiver-operating analysis, with areas under the curve of 0.9 and about 0.8 for the three pairwise comparisons — though the paper’s abstract and its results paragraph assign the 0.9 to different pairs. Those figures carry the weight a single study earns: blinded sonographers, but one laboratory, one vibration frequency from an off-the-shelf massager, sites chosen by palpation, and no pain-free controls. Color Doppler found prominent vessels near the points, and [arteries within a centimeter or two of active points showed a pulsatility index — how sharply flow surges and falls with each heartbeat — of 8.3, against 3.0 near normal sites]{claim=VASO-C031}, with flow running backward between heartbeats at 55 percent of active sites. That is the finding proponents read as the footprint of something clenched upstream.

The same paper contains the qualifiers. [Backward diastolic flow also appeared near 31 percent of palpably normal sites]{claim=VASO-C032}, so the waveform is a gradient across symptomatic muscle rather than a marker of a knot. [The resistivity index — a companion measure of downstream resistance — did not differ at all between active, latent and normal sites]{claim=VASO-C036}, and the pulsatility index varied so widely that it could not classify any individual site. There was no pain-free control group: the “normal” sites were five centimeters away in a muscle that had a trigger point somewhere else, and the authors say their flow findings “do not represent the normal variation.” The vessels interrogated were pulsatile arteries typically more than a millimeter across — not the microvessels a latch account would need. And the authors list, as candidate causes of the high-resistance flow, muscle contracture compressing the capillary bed, the anatomy of the trapezius apex, inflammatory vasoconstriction, and pressure from the transducer itself; they never mention smooth-muscle latch.

A second laboratory adds a second muscle. In 2025 Landfald, Podgórski and Olewnik examined thirty amateur runners with trigger points in the gastrocnemius — 103 points, 67 active and 36 latent — using B-mode ultrasound and strain elastography, a compression method rather than vibration. Active points were more painful than latent ones (8.9 against 6.1 on a ten-point scale), larger in cross-section (28 against 17 square millimeters) and stiffer relative to the surrounding muscle (stiffness ratio 8.5 against 6.1). The comparison is active against latent within symptomatic runners — no palpably normal or pain-free sites, no Doppler, no biochemistry — so it parallels the trapezius ordering in a different tissue by a different method without adding the control the trapezius work lacked; the ledger holds these differences as context beside the general claim that points differ from surrounding tissue, not as a replication. A 2021 systematic review of 33 imaging studies, characterized in this ledger only second-hand, reports that stiffness and flow measures can distinguish active and latent points from healthy tissue, with reproducibility caveats attached. The sum: palpated knots are stiffer than their surroundings, in a graded way, inside the muscle itself, and the local arteries behave somewhat differently — but the vascular signature is partial, the stiffness gradient comes from one laboratory with palpation-selected sites, and nothing in any of it says what the stiff tissue is.

Then there is the phenomenology practitioners report, which any candidate mechanism must explain. The obstruction feels like a dull blockage rather than a sharp stretch-pain. By the essay’s report, knots accumulate over years and hold flexibility hostage. And — the strange one — [pressure locates a knot, but release comes with breath: press in, exhale slowly, and something lets go within seconds]{claim=VASO-C004}. Practitioners add that [pressure alone, without the breath, does not release the point]{claim=VASO-C039} — the “two-key” rule — that fresh knots yield in a session and old ones take months, and that releasing an old, heavily loaded cluster can bring a wave of warmth and euphoria; this case catalogues those last reports as untested claims. The release itself enters the ledger as first-person testimony from the hypothesis’s own proponent, in an essay whose text was generated by AI models at the author’s direction; consistent with widespread practitioner lore, contradicted by no one, measured by no one. It is real evidence that people *feel* a release. It is no evidence at all that anything happens in the tissue.

The two-key rule has a published counter-example beside it, though not a graded one. The runners’ study released its trigger points by compression alone — thumb pressure in thirty-second bouts with ten-second rests, up to three rounds — and the ledger’s one record on the point states that no breathing instruction, recording or manipulation appears anywhere in its methods or results. What that protocol achieved is held in this ledger against a different question, the difference between active and latent points: after the first round, 86 percent of latent points and 60 percent of active ones were no longer detectable sonographically, and active points needed more sessions (1.4 against 1.1); the authors offer, as their own conjecture, that latent points may be “earlier or less fibrotic lesions.” Set side by side, the omission and the outcome look like a direct test of the two-key rule, and this edition reads them as a lead against it — an inference of the edition, marked as such, not a grade. The record admitted on the two-key claim says what the protocol omitted; what it achieved is held against the active/latent question; and this case does not spend a record admitted on one claim as a finding on another. So the claim stands *unresolved*, held on its proponent’s testimony. The question would stay open even on the most charitable reading: breathing was not held constant, and a runner under painful thumb pressure may well exhale slowly without being told to, so “no breath instruction” is not “breath excluded”; the endpoint was a stiff focus no longer visible after a round of compression lasting minutes, not a release timed to an exhale; the muscle and population differ from the practitioner reports; and the study performed no Doppler and archived no elastography cine loops, so the order in which blood and stiffness changed was not observed. What the admitted records do establish is that an imaged trigger point can become undetectable within a single session of pressure, over minutes, without anyone asking the subject to breathe — which is itself not scar.

## Two experiments that catch the loop in motion

The evidence that these spots are under ongoing neural control has existed for decades, largely unread. In 1993, Hubbard and Berkoff inserted fine needle electrodes into trapezius trigger points and, simultaneously, into adjacent non-tender fibers. They recorded sustained spontaneous electrical activity in a one-to-two-millimeter nidus of every trigger point, and none in the non-tender sites, with higher amplitude in tension-headache and fibromyalgia patients than in healthy subjects. The knot is not merely stiffer than its surroundings; it is a small island of maintained activity in muscle nominally at rest. The authors guessed that sympathetically driven muscle-spindle contractions were the source; later literature favors endplate potentials; the generator remains contested.

“None in the non-tender sites” needs a qualifier. Skeletal muscle fibers receive their nerve supply in a band called the motor endplate zone, and faint electrical activity there — endplate noise — is a known finding. In 2002 Simons, Hong and Simons located the endplate zone electrically in eleven muscles of ten subjects and needled three kinds of site. Endplate noise appeared at all eleven trigger-point sites; [it also appeared at four of eleven non-tender sites that lay in the endplate zone but outside any trigger point]{claim=VASO-C034}; and [it never appeared at taut-band sites outside the endplate zone]{claim=VASO-C035}. The authors’ own summary is that the signature is “characteristic of, but is not restricted to,” the trigger point. Put the two studies together and the honest statement is that [trigger points carry a sustained electrical signature more often than non-tender sites in the same endplate zone, and never where there is no endplate zone at all]{claim=VASO-C002} — a prevalence gradient, eleven of eleven against four of eleven against none, rather than an exclusive island. Hubbard and Berkoff’s silent control sites may simply have lain off the endplate zone. The Simons study was small, nonrandomized and unblinded, and its authors are the construct’s leading proponents; the finding nonetheless cuts against exclusivity, and it says where the signature lives: in the endplate zone first, and at the trigger point second.

The follow-up to Hubbard and Berkoff, from McNulty, Gevirtz, Hubbard and Berkoff in 1994, is the remarkable one. With electrodes in place in fourteen subjects, they administered mental arithmetic. [Activity at the trigger point rose; control sites in the same muscle stayed comparatively quiet; the subjects were not tensing]{claim=VASO-C003}. A purely mental event, involving no movement, turned up the signal inside one tender point and not a centimeter away. The brain has the knot’s address. Both studies are small, old, from one lineage, and never replicated with modern instrumentation; neither took any vascular measurement; and neither placed its control needle in a matched endplate-zone site, so whether the stressor selected the trigger point or simply any endplate zone is open. Two follow-ups from the same lineage — relaxation training lowering the activity, and an infusion of the alpha-blocker phentolamine quieting the site — are reported in the founding essay; candidate papers have been located but not retrieved, and until one is, the autonomic-maintenance argument rests on stress induction alone. Three readings of this one result are live: stress-sensitive endplates (guarding), a sympathetic write to an arteriole inside the muscle (the latch account), and [a regional sympathetic vasoconstriction written to a skin territory, as in blushing or blanching]{claim=VASO-C143} (the perforator account — a reading the ledger holds only as its proponent states it, in a source it has not been able to read). The needle cannot tell them apart. A skin-perfusion camera over the point during the arithmetic could.

Then, in August 2026, a study in *Nature Human Behaviour* supplied the regulatory counterpart. Mizrachi, Rottem and Rozenkrantz induced identical histamine skin-prick inflammation in the same fifty-seven volunteers on different occasions, in preregistered experiments, manipulating only where attention went. [Attending to the inflamed site produced roughly 1.5-fold smaller and faster-resolving wheal-and-flare responses in about ninety percent of participants across two cohorts — with no difference in skin conductance, heart rate, skin temperature or self-reported anxiety, and heart-rate variability higher under inward attention]{claim=VASO-C006}. A local anesthetic dissected two routes: a sensory one that lidocaine degraded and a top-down vagal one that survived it. What this shows is that cognition can write to a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site without arousal. What it does not show is anything about knots, smooth muscle, or seconds: the timescale was tens of minutes and the route is vagal immune regulation, in a tissue the authors note the parasympathetic system does not directly innervate. It is an existence proof for a channel, not for any of the featured mechanisms.

## The ratchet in the vessel walls

{plate:IMG-VASO-P02}

The body contains a second muscular system under no direct voluntary command: smooth muscle, lining the blood vessels, gut and airways, answering to autonomic state. Smooth muscle has a property skeletal muscle lacks, textbook physiology since Hai and Murphy formalized it in 1988: [the latch-bridge state, in which its molecular motors grip and then lock, holding tension at a small fraction of the usual energetic cost after the activating signal has faded]{claim=VASO-C010}. In the model, cross-bridges that have been switched off chemically — dephosphorylated — remain attached and detach only slowly, so a vessel can sustain high stress at low levels of activation. Low, not zero: the popular version, in which the signal “disappears entirely and the grip remains,” overstates what the model claims. Arteries must hold tone for a lifetime; the latch is how they afford it. The founding essay adds that latched tissue looks normal under a microscope and that the state is history-dependent; both are held here on the essay’s word, with no record behind either. A cheap, history-dependent hold that persists after its input fades is, in engineering terms, a memory element. Two questions follow. Is anything ever written to it? And does it exist in the vessels a knot would need?

Here the speed of the felt release becomes the crucial clue. Structural change in tissue — remodeling, scarring — takes days to weeks. [A change that completes in seconds, mid-exhale, must be a change of maintained state, not of structure]{claim=VASO-C011}: something the body is doing and can stop doing. Scar tissue does not release on an exhale. The inference is sound, and this case grades it as provisionally supported on physiological priors rather than on any time-resolved record — with two caveats. Its premise, that the felt release corresponds to an objective local event within seconds, is precisely the thing never measured; the closest the ledger comes is the runners’ stiff focus becoming undetectable over a session of minutes, and a small pilot in the trapezius work where three needled points shrank and their pulsatility index fell over subsequent visits. Both show the measures move; neither films seconds. And “state” is a bigger tent than “vascular”: sustained motor guarding is a state; so is fascial densification — the proposal, from fascia researchers, that [viscous hyaluronan between fascial layers thickens and then thins again under pressure, movement and warmth]{claim=VASO-C077}. If densification can reverse within a session, the knot could be a state without being a vessel — and pressure alone would be exactly what one would expect to work. Nobody in this ledger has retrieved the timescale; the claim is held on its anchor alone, which is why the research agenda asks for it.

## What the arteriole record actually says

This is where the case’s own study lands, and it lands against the comfortable assumption. A frozen-criteria evidence map (study VASO-S001) asked a narrow question: where, by vessel type and caliber, has the latch actually been demonstrated with a contemporaneous readout of activation or energetic cost? Sixteen eligible rows, 1981 to 2022, answered three ways.

First, the energetic argument — that a knot could be held for almost nothing — rests entirely on large conduit arteries. Every measurement of oxygen consumption, lactate release or ATP turnover during maintained force comes from swine or porcine carotid preparations held at zero transmural pressure. No arteriole or resistance microvessel of any bed has ever had its holding cost measured.

Second, the compartment the original hypothesis names has been examined, and what was found does not look like a latch. Three rows are pressurized rat skeletal-muscle arterioles — cremaster and gracilis, roughly a hundred micrometers across — in which myosin light-chain phosphorylation, the molecular marker of activation, was measured against diameter. In all three, maintained constriction came with maintained or *rising* phosphorylation: 27.7 percent at 30 mmHg rising to 39.6 percent at 120 mmHg in one study; about 40 percent at 10 mmHg rising to about 55 percent at 80 mmHg in another, attributed to calcium sensitization and actin polymerization. A 2000 paper states that arteriolar tone “represents a state of maintained smooth muscle activation that requires increases in [Ca2+]i and myosin light-chain phosphorylation.” That is the opposite signature to the economical, dephosphorylated hold a latch requires. The cautions are real: none of the three was designed as a latch test; all held their stimulus present throughout, so they could not have seen input-free persistence even if it exists; and the rows were built from abstracts. But the assumption that the arteriole was simply unexamined is gone.

Third, latch behavior is not generic across vascular smooth muscle. The one published comparison between a vessel and its own downstream branch — rabbit femoral artery against its saphenous branch — found sustained stress at falling calcium in the parent (42 percent phosphorylation) and a forty-percent stress loss in the branch (28 percent), attributed to motor-protein isoforms that do not support latch-bridge formation. One laboratory, one pair of papers, and nobody has followed the comparison further downstream.

So the mechanism the knot hypothesis borrows is real where it has been studied, and unobserved — arguably pointed away from — where the original hypothesis needs it. That is not a refutation. It is a mismatch, and a specific gap. It is also the reason a second vascular account exists that does not need the latch at all.

## What if blood talks back?

In 2008 the neuroscientists Christopher Moore and Rosa Cao proposed the hemo-neural hypothesis: that coupling between neurons and blood runs both ways — that [local vascular and hemodynamic state can modulate what nearby neurons do]{claim=VASO-C012}, through mechanical, thermal and chemical channels. It was a hypothesis paper; it demonstrated nothing new. Sixteen years later, in 2024, Jammal Salameh and colleagues reported in *Science* that physiological blood-pressure pulsations modulate central neuronal activity through mechanosensitive ion channels, in rat preparations and awake animals, on rapid timescales. The read path has a demonstrated mechanism. It is a mechanism of *instantaneous* modulation, in rat brain: it shows vessels can nudge neurons now, not that vessels can store anything and read it back later. Proponents argue that nothing in the logic is brain-specific and that peripheral sensory endings sit alongside the very vessels whose caliber they would sense. That extension is argument, not yet measurement.

## The synthesis, and what it would explain

The researcher Michael Edward Johnson has assembled these pieces into a program he calls vasocomputation, stated in three hypotheses of ascending ambition: that rhythmic vessel contraction acts as a compression sweep collapsing ambiguous neural patterns; that a vascular contraction freezes local neural patterns for its duration, functioning as a prediction and a medium-term memory; and that a contraction held long enough engages the latch and durably freezes nearby circuitry until the prediction resolves. Write, store, read: [vascular tension as a memory medium participating in mental life — with the grasping Buddhism calls tanha as its felt signature]{claim=VASO-C021}. The program is self-published, not peer-reviewed, and as of 2026 its experiments seek evidence rather than report it. The critical report commissioned for this case adds the sharpest objection: biological memory requires a state that depends on prior input, can later be read out, and discriminates between different prior inputs. A thermostat has hysteresis; it does not have an autobiography. The latch literature addresses none of these criteria, and the report notes that the nearest genuine write–store–read loop in a living flow network is a slime mold storing nutrient locations in the diameters of its own tubes — an organism very unlike us.

Whatever the fate of that grand identification, consider what the stack offers the humble knot. [A knot becomes a latched arteriole throttling its own neighborhood — chronic local ischemia at near-zero energetic cost, producing the acidic, sensitized milieu the microdialysis found, wrapped in secondary skeletal-muscle guarding]{claim=VASO-C020}. This would patch the oldest hole in trigger-point theory: the classic “energy crisis” model needed muscle fibers in permanent maximal contraction, a metabolic bonfire no one could account for, where a latch holds for almost nothing. It would explain why knots feel like autonomous objects, why they persist for years, why the Doppler findings show flow behaving as if something upstream were clenched — remembering that the Doppler authors list contracture compressing the bed as a candidate cause. And it would explain the two-key protocol. Smooth muscle takes no voluntary commands, but it answers to autonomic state, and [slow breathing with extended exhalation reproducibly shifts autonomic balance toward the parasympathetic]{claim=VASO-C013} — a 2018 systematic review documents the rise in heart-rate variability and respiratory sinus arrhythmia across studies of healthy people. Pressure perturbs the local loop; breath shifts the chemistry that governs unlatching. The roller is the read head; the exhale is the write head. Note what the breathing evidence establishes: a global shift, measured on the heart, in people with no tender point in the study. The local, site-specific unlatching the hypothesis adds on top has never been measured — and the runners’ protocol cleared points with the breath half never instructed.

## Three accounts of a knot, side by side

Strip the case to its live mechanisms and there are three — two vascular, one not — and they make different predictions about the same seconds-long event and about what pressure alone should do.

### The latched arteriole

*What it proposes.* A microvessel inside the muscle, held shut by smooth-muscle latch, starving a small territory; the electrical nidus, the acid and the guarding are downstream. *What it predicts.* A stiff, electrically active spot that is metabolically *cold* on FDG-PET, because a latch burns almost nothing; a latch-competent motor-protein phenotype in skeletal-muscle arterioles; at a release, blood returning before stiffness falls; and a breath-gated release, since the autonomic shift is what picks the lock. *What the ledger holds.* The latch is real in conduit arteries; the arteriole record shows maintained activation, not a latch; no arteriole’s holding cost has ever been measured; the vessels with abnormal Doppler are conduit-scale; the critical report finds no study identifying smooth-muscle latch at any tender point; and a pressure-only protocol with no breath instruction cleared points in the calf over minutes. Its reply to the last is that pressure itself perturbs the local loop and that uninstructed breathing is not held breath. *What would decide it.* A pressurized skeletal-muscle arteriole holding constriction after its stimulus is withdrawn, at falling phosphorylation; a cold knot on PET; a release blocked by an inhale-and-hold — or, against it, a hot knot, the non-latching phenotype all the way down, and equal release under held breath.

### The stuck perforator

*What it proposes.* A second account, set out in the proponent’s companion essay of September 2026, accepts the arteriole audit and moves the vascular element up and out — from arterioles inside the muscle to the small artery-nerve-lymphatic bundles that pierce the superficial fascia on their way to the skin, which surgeons call perforators and locate with a pencil Doppler. A knot, on this picture, is a perforator held in a stuck state, and [what holds it is not one memory element but three, nested: the vessel’s tone, a collar of gelled hyaluronan around the bundle, and the tether the collar makes between the fascial sheet and the tissue beneath]{claim=VASO-C174}, each staying where it was put after the input that put it there has gone. The essay holds the skin’s arterioles to be among the most sympathetically dominated vessels in the body, so that the bed needs no economical latch; ordinary tonic firing suffices. *What it predicts.* That palpated tender points coincide with Doppler-mapped perforators above chance. That the “star” or spark felt at a release is reperfusion tingling in the skin patch one perforator supplies. That the breath works through what the essay calls a textbook reflex — a deep inspiration constricting skin arterioles within about two seconds, a slow exhale letting them reopen — so that pressure applied during an inhale-and-hold should fail. That freeing the collar with a few milliliters of saline under ultrasound should release a knot with no breath at all — which means this account, unlike the latch account, can absorb pressure-alone release: pressure adds heat and shear to the collar. And, like the latch account, [blood first, stiffness second]{claim=VASO-C073} — at the skin surface, where a laser speckle camera can film it. *What the ledger holds.* Nothing, in either direction. Its only source is the proponent’s second essay, whose text was AI-generated and which this ledger has not been able to read and verify, so the records drawn from it carry no weight here; the published studies it invokes are catalogued as its propositions, not as retrieved records. It also owes an explanation of the one instrumented pattern that fits the intramuscular picture best: the stiff regions the sonographers report, in the trapezius and the calf, lie inside the muscle, not in the fascia under the skin. *What would decide it.* An afternoon with a pencil Doppler and two blinded operators — do the tender points sit on the perforators above chance? Then a hydrodissection trial and the inhale-hold block.

### Guarding, densification, and interpretation

*What it proposes.* Tender points are neuromuscular guarding: sustained low-level motor drive and endplate activity in skeletal muscle, centrally maintained and stress-sensitive, possibly with altered fascial gliding from hyaluronan densification. Nothing is stored in a vessel. The brain stops guarding, regionally or globally, and interpretation supplies the rest. *What it predicts.* That the electrical signature tracks the endplate zone rather than the tender point — which is what Simons found, in part; that a mental stressor raises activity at any endplate-zone site; that the chemistry and the Doppler waveforms follow from compression of the bed by contracted fiber — which the imaging authors list as a candidate cause; that pressure alone suffices to switch a point off and the breath adds nothing local — which is what the runners’ protocol, read at face value, suggests; that any fast mechanical change is densification thinning, with no perfusion change; that the sparks practitioners feel are hyperventilation paresthesias, tracking carbon dioxide and appearing at sham sites too; and that FDG uptake at knots is elevated. *What the ledger holds.* This account needs no new physiology, the only direct arteriole measurements available fit it better than a latch, and the only imaged within-session disappearance of a trigger point was obtained by pressure with breathing uninstructed. Its gap is the set of localized objective findings a purely central story must still explain: the stiff regions blinded sonographers report in two muscles, electrical activity a mental task turns up at one point and not a centimeter away, abnormal local chemistry and flow. And it shares one weakness with its rivals — the observation base it explains was located by palpation, whose reliability is unproven. *What would decide it.* The same experiments, read the other way: a matched endplate-zone control rising as much as the trigger point under arithmetic; stiffness dropping with no perfusion change; a hot knot on PET; release equal under held breath; sparks that track CO2 rather than the button press.

The three agree that people feel releases, that palpated points are stiffer than their surroundings, that slow breathing shifts autonomic state globally, and that a knot is a state rather than a scar. They part over *which* state, in *which* tissue, held by *what* — and over the same unfilmed seconds: blood before stiffness, or stiffness with no local perfusion change, or nothing local at all.

## The oldest anatomy text

{plate:IMG-VASO-P01}

Essentially every contemplative tradition that mapped the inner body arrived at the same three claims: there are knots, breath is the tool, and untying them changes consciousness. Tibetan tantric physiology describes channel-knots — rtsa mdud — constricting the flow of wind, untied by breath practice; Hindu yoga names the granthis; Chinese medicine records ashi points, tender spots named for the patient’s cry. The standard modern move is to file this as metaphor. The alternative reading is that [practitioners with extraordinarily trained interoception were producing first-person cartography of the vascular-autonomic tension system]{claim=VASO-C022} — channels as vasculature, winds as autonomic state, knots as latches or clenched bundles. The only record this ledger holds on the claim, in either direction, is the founding essay’s own uncited assertion that the traditional maps place the important knots along the torso’s midline and the limbs rather than in the head. The perforator essay sharpens the proposal — classical points as perforators, the “knotting” places of the Chinese sinew channels as the bony lines where the fascial sheet is anchored — and that sharpening is useful precisely because it can be coded blind and tested against chance. Nobody has done so. Until someone does, every convergence is vulnerable to post-hoc matching — and even a genuine alignment with vascular geography would not show that anything latches or clenches. The traditions also preserved a warning, which this case records without adopting a mechanism: releasing held material faster than the system can integrate is destabilizing.

## The crux, and what would change our mind

Strip everything away and the disagreement is narrower than any camp admits. It funnels into one empirical question: when a knot “releases” on a slow exhale, does anything objective happen locally — a stiffness drop, a perfusion rise, time-locked to the breath, exceeding what pressure alone, expectation, and generalized relaxation produce? Behind it sit two more. If something does happen, is the releasing element a vessel, and if so which one — an arteriole in the muscle or a perforator under the skin? And is the breath a key at all? On the third the ledger holds the lead described above rather than a grade, and the experiment that separates “breath necessary,” “breath gating” and “breath irrelevant” is whether an inhale-and-hold would block the clearance that pressure produced.

What would move this case toward a vascular account:

- Time-resolved imaging of a felt release showing stiffness falling and perfusion rising together within seconds of the exhale, at palpated sites but not sham sites, with the vascular ordering — blood first, stiffness second.
- Pressure applied during an inhale-and-hold failing to clear points that pressure during free or slow breathing clears — the breath-gating signature.
- A local flash of skin perfusion time-locked to the exhale and the felt star, absent at sham sites — the perforator signature.
- Blinded tender points coinciding with Doppler-mapped perforators above chance; a knot released by saline hydrodissection at its perforator with no breath.
- A pressurized skeletal-muscle arteriole holding constriction after its stimulus is withdrawn, with falling phosphorylation and measured low energetic cost.
- A palpated knot stiff on elastography and electrically active on EMG yet metabolically cold on FDG-PET.
- A retrieved primary study showing sympathetic blockade quiets the electrical nidus.
- A repeat of the mental-arithmetic experiment in which the trigger point rises and a matched endplate-zone control site does not — or a skin-perfusion fall over the point and not over control skin.
- In an animal, different induced vascular states producing reliably different later neural responses under identical stimulation, with oxygenation clamped.

What would move it toward the conventional account:

- Equal clearance of trigger points under held breath, slow exhalation and free breathing, all exceeding sham — pressure suffices and the exhale is a felt correlate.
- Felt releases without reproducible local transitions, or equal transitions at sham sites.
- Fascial densification reversing under pressure with no perfusion change — a fast, non-vascular state.
- Sparks whose perfusion correlates are global, equal at sham sites, and track carbon dioxide rather than the button press.
- Elevated FDG uptake at palpated knots.
- A matched endplate-zone control site rising as much as the trigger point under mental arithmetic.
- Tender points falling on perforators no more often than chance.
- A paired-caliber study finding the non-latching motor-protein phenotype throughout skeletal-muscle arterioles.
- A knot census with pain-free controls finding that Doppler and stiffness measures do not pick out the palpated spots.

## Where the ledger stands

The verdict is *unresolved*, and that is a finding rather than a shrug. The ladder is inverted: the best-evidenced rungs — the latch exists, slow breathing shifts the autonomic system, vessels can nudge neurons, palpated points are stiffer than their surroundings — are the least *diagnostic*, meaning they are exactly what conventional physiology predicts too and so decide nothing between the accounts. The rungs that would decide the case — that a release is objective within seconds, that the releasing element is vascular — have no time-resolved evidence in either direction. The two-key claim is graded unresolved with care, for the reasons given where the runners’ protocol is described; the lead against it does not touch state-not-scar — if anything it strengthens it — but it puts the breath’s standing as a necessary key in question, and with it the cleanest argument that the releasing element must answer to autonomic state. Several featured claims — the blood-first ordering, the reversibility of densification, the perforator account and its skin-territory write — are held on their anchors alone: the ledger knows where each is stated and has admitted no weighed observation behind it, and because a source is not evidence, each grades unresolved for that reason and no other. The claim most exposed on the vascular side is the knot-as-latched-arteriole attribution, because the arteriole record leans against it and the vascular footprint at real trigger points is partial. The perforator account has nothing behind it but a proponent’s unread essay — featured because it is a genuinely different mechanism with cheap tests, not because anything supports it. The observation most easily misread is the electrical nidus: real, stress-reactive, but more common at trigger points rather than exclusive to them, and living in the endplate zone. The claim the whole case hangs from is the felt release, credible as an experience and worthless, on its own, as a mechanism. And the case’s opening sentence — that the points are common across the population — is graded only weakly supported: the ledger holds their occurrence, in patients and in two people with no pain, and holds their frequency on no measurement at all.

The strongest argument for the vascular hypothesis that this verdict does not answer deserves stating plainly. The classic energy-crisis account has never explained how a fiber stays maximally contracted for years without exhausting itself; a latch would, and a clenched skin arteriole, which the body already pays to hold all day, would not need to. The electrical signature is millimeter-scale and stress-reactive while surrounding muscle stays quiet, which is odd for diffuse guarding even if the signature also appears at a minority of other endplate-zone sites. Blinded sonographers in two laboratories report stiff regions at exactly the sites examiners palpate, and the arteries nearby behave differently. Attention has been shown to regulate a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site without arousal. Every arteriole study that found maintained activation kept its stimulus on, so none could have seen a state that persists after input stops. The runners whose trigger points cleared under thumb pressure were never told how to breathe, and a person in pain under sustained pressure tends to exhale — the inhale-hold arm that would settle it has not been run. The perforator version, as its proponent states it, asks for no new physiology: a skin bed he reads as breath-gated in seconds by textbook reflex and site-addressable by ordinary blushing. And the hypothesis makes a timing prediction no rival makes — perfusion changes before stiffness — which is falsifiable and cheap. None of this is evidence that knots are vessels. It is a reason the experiments are worth running.

## The research agenda

The keystone experiment — ultrafast elastography and sensitive Doppler over a palpated knot, sites fixed in advance by blinded examiners, calibrated pressure through an instrumented probe, factorial controls, a button press at each felt release, and a mental-arithmetic block to catch stiffening during a purely cognitive event — would cost less than a mid-size grant and has never been run. It leads the open program. Second is the cheapest test the ledger has earned: repeat the runners’ compression protocol with breathing recorded and randomized point by point — free breathing, instructed slow exhalation, pressure only during an inhale-and-hold — with sham compression at a non-tender site and an untreated point followed alongside, cine loops archived and Doppler added. If held breath does not lower the clearance rate, the breath is not a key; if it blocks clearance while the exhale matches or beats free breathing, the breath-gating both vascular accounts predict is real; if every active arm beats sham equally, pressure suffices and the exhale is a correlate. Then the laser speckle camera over a knot on the occiput or upper trapezius with exhale, inhale-hold, sham-site and carbon-dioxide controls; the paired-caliber arteriole study with a stimulus-withdrawal phase; the retrieval of the still-unopened primaries, above all the phentolamine and relaxation papers; the mental-arithmetic repeat with a matched endplate-zone control; the perforator coincidence map; the hydrodissection trial; the densification timescale; the FDG-PET overlay; the factorial eight-to-twelve-week trial separating the probe from the permission; the remaining community tender-point surveys, since the retrieved one is pain-selected and an unselected sample is what a proto-census needs; the census nobody has taken, with pain-free controls, children and long-term meditators; the animal experiment separating vascular memory from vascular plumbing; the blinded coding of the contemplative maps; the knot-free practitioner as a natural experiment, with a sensory exam to rule out a numbed finder; and the retrieval of the primaries behind the euphoria reports and the perforator essay’s citations. One item is done: the evidence map of the latch by vessel type and caliber was executed as the study reported above — its finding is what moved the vascular idea out of the arteriole in the first place. A full-body ultrasound scanner announced in 2026 makes whole-body coverage imaginable, but it is a prototype built for body composition, not for the stiffness and flow channels a census needs.

The machines and the practitioners exist; the experiments are small and specified. Someone should count. Until someone does, how common the knot is rests on the roller’s word and the essay’s. Press into one, if you find one — and, for now, breathe however you like; whether the exhale matters is exactly the question.

assessment.synthesis: The ladder stays inverted. The best-evidenced rungs are the mechanism rungs — the latch-bridge model on VASO-C010 (VASO-E003), the slow-breathing autonomic shift on VASO-C013 (VASO-E009), mechanosensitive vascular-to-neural modulation in rat brain on VASO-C012 (VASO-E005) — and each is credible without being diagnostic, because guarding, densification and ordinary physiology predict each of them too. The observation base rests on four primaries. On VASO-C005, Shah 2008 gives the biochemistry (VASO-E006), the Mazza review, characterized second-hand, gives group-level stiffness and flow differences (VASO-E007), and Ballyns 2011 gives two instrumented findings: a group-level Doppler difference (VASO-E022, also on VASO-C031 and VASO-C032) and the vibration-elastography stiff-area gradient — active and latent areas significantly above normal (VASO-E091), the normal-site value (VASO-E090), the active-versus-normal classifier (VASO-E096), the active-versus-latent classifier (VASO-E099) and the overall ROC separation (VASO-E100, VASO-E102), with the abstract's own ROC listing (VASO-E101, VASO-E103) read as context because it assigns the 0.9 to a different pair than the results paragraph does. The two trigger-point means carry VASO-C182 (VASO-E087, VASO-E089; VASO-E093, VASO-E106 and the calf parallel VASO-E085 as context) and the normal-site mean carries VASO-C187 (VASO-E090; VASO-E104, VASO-E105 and VASO-E107), so both grade provisionally supported rather than anchor-only: blinded sonographers, but one laboratory, one vibration frequency, palpation-selected sites, and the same NIH lineage as the biochemistry. The same source caps its own findings — no pain-free controls and retrograde flow at 31% of palpably normal sites (VASO-E026, on VASO-C005, VASO-C031 and VASO-C032), flow indices that cannot classify sites (VASO-E025, on VASO-C005), a null resistivity index on VASO-C036 (VASO-E024); on VASO-C020 its authors list contracture compression as a co-equal cause of the flow pattern, so VASO-E027 is weighed at zero diagnosticity. Landfald 2025 adds a second laboratory, muscle and method on VASO-C005: pain, area and stiffness-ratio differences between active and latent points (VASO-E069, VASO-E070, VASO-E071) and first-round sonographic disappearance of 60% of active and 86% of latent points (VASO-E072), all within symptomatic runners with no control tissue, which is why those records are context and qualifier rather than support; on VASO-C030 the authors state the reliability problem in their own words and report that imaging confirmed 71.5% of palpated spots (VASO-E078, VASO-E079, VASO-E081). On VASO-C001 the ledger separates two propositions the claim bundles: occurrence is documented — Croft 1994 found fixed-site tender points in two people reporting no pain, in a pain-selected subsample (VASO-E082, VASO-E083, both context) — while commonness across the general population is held only on the essay's own report (VASO-E015) and a 1986 clinic estimate quoted second-hand (VASO-E028), with VASO-E012 qualifying even the palpable spot; the claim grades weakly supported at low confidence, its frequency half unmeasured. On VASO-C002, Simons 2002 (VASO-E031) makes the electrical nidus a prevalence gradient rather than an exclusive island, and on VASO-C034 and VASO-C035 (VASO-E032) places the signature in the endplate zone first; read beside VASO-C003's single record (VASO-E002), that exposes an unmatched control site — an inference across claims, stated as one. The anchor observation, a seconds-scale release on an exhale (VASO-C004), is supported only by proponent testimony (VASO-E014). On VASO-C039 the claim's one admitted record (VASO-E067, direction context) establishes that a published pressure-only protocol carried no breathing instruction, recording or manipulation — and nothing more. What that protocol achieved is held on VASO-C005 (VASO-E072), over a course of up to three thirty-second compressions — minutes, not the seconds of the felt release — so it is named here as a lead and not spent as a grade on a claim it is not attached to; the two-key necessity grades unresolved at low confidence, held on its anchor. Where the original thesis needs the latch, the record on VASO-C020 points the other way: pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles show maintained or rising phosphorylation (VASO-E020), no arteriole energetic measurement exists (VASO-E019), and the report's audit finds no latch identified at any tender point (VASO-E016); on VASO-C010 the one paired comparison lost latch behaviour one branch order downstream (VASO-E021). The essay-derived records (VASO-E033, VASO-E034, VASO-E035, VASO-E036, VASO-E037, VASO-E038, VASO-E041, VASO-E042, VASO-E043) are restatements or hypothesis statements at zero independent weight; VASO-E039 is the sole record on VASO-C022 and leaves it untested. The records drawn from the second essay (VASO-E044, VASO-E045, VASO-E050, VASO-E051, VASO-E052) rest on a source the ledger has not read and are treated as absent; the perforator account (VASO-C174, with VASO-C143 as its write mechanism and VASO-C073 as its timing prediction) sits on the map on its anchor alone, as does densification's reversibility (VASO-C077). The memory attribution (VASO-C021) fails the write–store–read test (VASO-E017). Sensitivity: no single removal flips the case verdict, because neither direction holds decisive time-resolved evidence. The record whose removal would most change the case is VASO-E020: without it the arteriole compartment reverts to unexamined and the original thesis loses its principal contrary finding. VASO-E031 most constrains the reading of the observations. Unresolved is a finding, not a default: three accounts of the same event are specified, the decisive experiments are cheap and unrun, and the one natural test the ledger holds — pressure without breath — awaits a breath-controlled repeat before it can be read on the claim it would decide.
assessment.steelman: The classic energy-crisis account of trigger points has never explained how a skeletal-muscle fiber could remain near-maximally contracted for years without exhausting itself; a latch is the one known physiological device that holds tension for almost nothing, and a clenched skin arteriole, which the body demonstrably pays to hold all day, would not even need the economy — so the puzzle the conventional account cannot dissolve is exactly the one both vascular accounts dissolve. The electrical signature is confined to one to two millimeters and is selectively turned up by mental arithmetic while surrounding muscle stays quiet; that it also appears at four of eleven other endplate-zone sites does not explain why it is present at eleven of eleven trigger points, nor why a stressor picks the tender one. Blinded sonographers in two laboratories report stiff regions at exactly the sites examiners palpate — graded active above latent above palpably normal in the trapezius, each step now an admitted record — and the arteries nearby behave differently: the footprint a throttled bed would leave, whatever else could leave it. Voluntary attention has been shown, in preregistered human experiments, to regulate a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site with no change in arousal — the write channel the synthesis needs, demonstrated. Every arteriole study reporting maintained activation held its stimulus present throughout, so none could have detected a state that persists after input stops, which is the only state a knot requires. The one published pressure-only protocol never told its runners how to breathe and never recorded their breathing; a person under painful sustained pressure tends to exhale, so whatever that protocol cleared over its minutes of compression is compatible with the exhale doing the work uninstructed, and the arm that would exclude that reading — pressure applied only during an inhale-and-hold — has not been run. The perforator version, as its proponent states it, asks for no new physiology at all: he reads the skin bed as constricted by a deep breath within two seconds by a textbook reflex, opened by a slow exhale, addressed site by site every time a person blushes, and history-dependent after cold — and he points to a class of exquisitely tender points medicine already recognizes where a vessel-nerve bundle pierces a fascial ring, relieved by freeing the ring; none of that is yet an admitted record here, but none of it is exotic. Finally, the vascular hypothesis makes distinctive, falsifiable predictions that neither guarding nor densification makes — perfusion rises before stiffness falls; release blocked by held breath; a knot released by hydrodissection without breath; a stiff, active spot that is metabolically cold — and all of them can be tested for the cost of a small grant, one of them by adding a respiration belt to a protocol that already exists. None of this shows that knots are vessels; it is the best reason the assessment cannot yet be closed against them.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: Muscle knots are maintained vascular-autonomic states rather than structural lesions. In the form the case grades, the state is microvascular smooth muscle inside the muscle held in the latch-bridge state, throttling local blood flow and sensitizing local nerve endings, with secondary skeletal-muscle guarding layered on top; the knot is said to be writable by stress, readable as stiffness and ache, and releasable by sustained pressure combined with slow exhalation. The features the admitted evidence carries for that thesis are these: active points differ chemically from surrounding tissue; blinded sonographers in the upper trapezius find a graded region of stiffness — a larger area at active than at latent points, and both classes significantly larger than palpably normal sites — that separates site classes on ROC analysis, from one laboratory with palpation-selected sites and no pain-free controls; a systematic imaging review, characterized second-hand, reports stiffness and flow measures that distinguish points from healthy tissue, and in the calf the more symptomatic class of point is larger, stiffer and more painful than the less symptomatic class; the arteries near trapezius points show partially abnormal flow; a millimeter-scale electrical signature at trigger points is turned up by a purely mental stressor; smooth muscle can hold force cheaply after activation falls in conduit arteries; slow breathing shifts autonomic balance globally; vascular mechanics can modulate neurons in rat brain; and, on the active/latent question, imaged trigger points can become sonographically undetectable within a first round of pressure lasting minutes. What the admitted evidence does not carry, on the two-key claim itself, is the necessity of the breath: the one record admitted there establishes only that a published pressure-only protocol carried no breathing instruction. Nor does it carry the commonness of tender points across the general population: their occurrence is documented, their frequency is held on the essay's report and a second-hand clinic estimate. Held here on its anchor only, in a source the ledger has not read, is a second form from the same proponent: the state is a cutaneous perforator — a small artery, nerve and lymphatic passing together through a ring in the superficial fascia — held constricted by ordinary sympathetic tone, collared by gelled hyaluronan and tethering the fascial sheet, needing no latch. More broadly, and on hypothesis statements alone, vascular tension is said to function as a memory element participating in mental life, the physical implementation of what contemplative traditions call clinging, and the traditional anatomies of knots and channels are said to be first-person maps of the same system.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether people feel tender spots, not over whether palpated points differ measurably from surrounding tissue at group level — blinded sonographers in two muscles report them stiffer, in a graded way — not over whether smooth muscle can latch, and not over state versus scar: all three live accounts say a knot is a state, and an imaged stiff focus that becomes undetectable within a session of compression is not scar. The crux is whether anything objective happens locally when a knot 'releases' on a slow exhale: does stiffness fall and perfusion rise within seconds, time-locked to the breath, beyond what pressure alone, expectation and generalized relaxation produce? Behind it sit three further disputes. Which tissue holds the state: an arteriole inside the muscle (where the published record shows maintained activation, not a latch), a perforator under the skin (where nothing has been measured at all), a stress-sensitive skeletal endplate under central guarding, or gelled fascial hyaluronan? Is the breath a key at all — the one rung where the ledger holds a natural test it has not admitted as an observation on the claim: a pressure-only protocol with no breathing instruction whose minutes-scale outcomes are recorded against the active/latent question, leaving open whether held breath would have blocked them? And does the brain address the knot or merely the endplate zone, given that the electrical signature also appears at a minority of non-tender endplate-zone sites? Beneath all of it, the skeptical literature disputes whether the trigger point is reliably identifiable at all — the one study that checked found imaging confirmed about three-quarters of what an examiner palpated, while the stiffness gradient itself was measured at sites the examiner had already chosen — and how common the points are outside symptomatic muscle has never been measured.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: A time-locked imaging experiment: ultrafast shear-wave elastography and sensitive microvascular Doppler over a palpated knot during breath-assisted release, with sites fixed in advance by blinded examiners, calibrated pressure through an instrumented probe, factorial controls (pressure with normal breathing, slow breathing without pressure, pressure during an inhale-and-hold, sham sites, failed attempts), a button press at each felt release, and a preregistered prediction that stiffness drops and perfusion rises together within seconds of the exhale, exceeding all controls, with perfusion leading stiffness. Felt releases without reproducible local transitions, or equal transitions at shams and under pressure alone, would return the knot to the guarding-and-interpretation account. The cheapest decisive companion is specified: repeat the runners' single-session compression protocol with breathing recorded and randomized point by point across free breathing, instructed slow exhalation and pressure only during an inhale-and-hold, with sham and untreated arms, cine loops archived and Doppler added — if held breath does not lower clearance, the breath is not a key; if it blocks clearance, breath-gating is real. That study would also supply, as admitted atomic observations, the pressure-only outcome the two-key claim now lacks on its own records. A surface variant with laser speckle contrast imaging and end-tidal CO2 discriminates the perforator, hyperventilation and no-local-event readings at once. Companion studies decide the compartment and the localization: a blinded pencil-Doppler coincidence map of tender points against perforators; ultrasound-guided saline hydrodissection at a mapped perforator with no breath; a paired-caliber, pressurized arteriole preparation with a stimulus-withdrawal phase; a repeat of the mental-arithmetic experiment with a matched endplate-zone control site; a small FDG-PET overlay testing whether stiff, active knots are metabolically cold; a retrieved densification timescale; and a Doppler and elastography census with pain-free controls and sites fixed by instrument rather than thumb, since every existing stiffness and flow comparison sits inside symptomatic muscle at palpation-selected sites.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Tenderness and its relief need no vascular memory. Tender points are neuromuscular guarding — sustained low-level motor drive and endplate activity in skeletal muscle, centrally maintained and stress-sensitive — possibly with altered fascial gliding from hyaluronan densification between fascial layers. The electrical signature is endplate noise, a property of the endplate zone that is more prevalent where tissue is tender; a stressor that raises sympathetic drive to endplates would raise it. The stiff region blinded sonographers map at a palpated point is contracted fibre and guarding, graded with symptom severity because guarding is graded with symptom severity. The acidic, mediator-rich milieu follows from compression under guarding as readily as from a throttled vessel, and the high-resistance Doppler waveforms near trigger points are, by the imaging authors' own account, as compatible with contracture squeezing the capillary bed as with distal constriction — while a second resistance index shows no difference at all. Sustained pressure switches the guarding off or thins the densified lubricant, which is why a compression protocol with nobody told how to breathe made most latent and a majority of active imaged trigger points undetectable after one round of minutes-long compressions; the felt release on an exhale is expectation and attention doing what they demonstrably do, riding the genuine but global parasympathetic shift of slow breathing, with pressure altering local sensation. Any rapid mechanical change is densification thinning or guarding switching off, not a vessel unlatching or a perforator reopening; the sparks practitioners describe are, on this account, hyperventilation paresthesias, global and CO2-tracking rather than local. Nothing is stored locally: the brain stops guarding, regionally or globally, and interpretation supplies the rest. A stricter version adds that manual trigger-point identification has poor examiner reliability and no validated reference standard — imaging confirmed only about three-quarters of one examiner's palpated spots — so part of the observation base may be an artifact of training and expectation. This account requires no new physiology, and the only direct arteriole measurements available fit it better than they fit a latch. Its gap is the set of localized objective findings — the graded stiff regions blinded sonographers report in two muscles, spontaneous electrical activity that a mental task selectively raises at one point, abnormal local chemistry and flow — that a purely central or interpretive story must still account for.

inputs.title: Founding narrative (2026-09-01 snapshot)
inputs.text:
There is a strange gap at the center of musculoskeletal medicine. Anyone with a foam roller and twenty minutes can locate [dozens of small, discrete, exquisitely tender points in their own body]{claim=VASO-C001} — most densely around the hips and shoulders, more numerous with every passing decade. Roll across one and it announces itself unmistakably. Yet open the research literature and you will find scientists arguing about what these points are — and, in part, [about whether the "trigger point" is a real, reliably identifiable thing at all]{claim=VASO-C030}.

This case is about that gap, and about a chain of ideas that may close it — running from classical muscle physiology through a radical hypothesis about blood and thought, all the way to Tibetan contemplative anatomy. The chain starts on solid experimental ground and climbs into open speculation. The rungs are labeled along the way; the argument ladder below this article makes the decay visible.

## A phenomenon without a mechanism

Part of the reason the fight has run so long is structural. Modern medicine is organized by organ system: orthopedics owns bones, neurology owns nerves, cardiology owns the pipes. Nobody owns muscle tone — the continuous, neurally-set background contraction of soft tissue. No specialty means no billing codes, no imaging protocols, no funding lines. The skeptics' strongest argument — "there is no evidence" — is quietly circular: there is little evidence in part because no one has ever been paid to look properly. But the skeptical case deserves its full weight, and it is heavier than proponents usually grant: systematic reviews found that examiners cannot reliably agree on where trigger points are, there is no validated reference standard for what one is, and the most pointed peer-reviewed critique argues the whole construct rests on circular reasoning. The dispute is not only about mechanism. It reaches the observation base itself.

What survives the critique is a set of instrumented findings. Microdialysis at active trigger points found [the local fluid markedly acidic and loaded with pain mediators — substance P, CGRP, bradykinin]{claim=VASO-C005}; ultrasound studies report the sites stiffer than surrounding tissue, with abnormal local blood flow. Something is there, and it is chemically angry. And practitioners report a consistent phenomenology that any candidate mechanism must explain: the obstruction feels like a dull blockage rather than a sharp stretch-pain, as though the tissue layers themselves had stopped sliding; knots accumulate with age and hold flexibility hostage; and — the strange one — [pressure locates a knot, but release comes with breath: press in, exhale slowly, and something lets go in seconds]{claim=VASO-C004}. That last observation is first-person, from the case author's own practice among many others, and this case labels it as such: it is the anchor phenomenon of everything that follows, and no one has ever measured it.

## Two experiments that catch the loop in motion

The evidence that these spots are under direct neural control has existed for decades, largely unread. In 1993, Hubbard and Berkoff inserted fine needle electrodes into trapezius trigger points and recorded [continuous spontaneous electrical activity confined to a millimeter-scale nidus — chatter in muscle supposedly at rest, vanishing a centimeter away in non-tender tissue]{claim=VASO-C002}. The knot is not merely stiffer than its surroundings; it is a small island of maintained activity.

The follow-up, from McNulty, Gevirtz and colleagues in 1994, is the remarkable one. With electrodes in place, they gave subjects mental arithmetic. [Activity at the trigger point rose; activity at a control site in the same muscle did not; the subject was not tensing]{claim=VASO-C003}. A purely mental event, involving no movement, selectively turned up the electrical activity inside one tender point. The brain has the knot's address. Both studies are small, old, and from one lineage — but under every contested interpretation of what the chatter is, the core finding survives: a discrete tender spot maintained by ongoing neural activity, dialed up by stress.

And in August 2026, a study in Nature Human Behaviour supplied the regulatory counterpart. Mizrachi and colleagues induced identical histamine skin-prick inflammation in the same people twice, manipulating only where attention went. [Attending to the inflamed site produced roughly 1.5-fold smaller, faster-resolving responses in about 90% of participants — with no difference in arousal, and heart-rate variability rising under internal attention]{claim=VASO-C006}. Cognition can write tension into a specific peripheral site; attention and its autonomic train can regulate peripheral physiology back down. The loop's existence is no longer speculative. What remains speculative is what, physically, does the holding.

## The ratchet in the vessel walls

{plate:IMG-VASO-P02}

The body contains a second muscular system under no direct voluntary control: smooth muscle, lining the blood vessels, gut, and airways. Smooth muscle has a property skeletal muscle lacks, textbook physiology since Hai and Murphy formalized it in 1988: [the latch-bridge state, in which its molecular motors grip and then lock, holding tension at a small fraction of the energetic cost after the activating signal has faded]{claim=VASO-C010}. Arteries must hold tone for a lifetime; the latch is how they afford it. It is a kinetic trap, not damage — latched tissue looks normal under a microscope. It is remote-controlled by autonomic state: stress chemistry makes latches form more easily, and the relaxation pathways actively pick the locks. And it exhibits hysteresis — the tissue's present state depends on its history. A cheap, history-dependent hold that persists after its input vanishes is, in engineering terms, a memory element. The question is whether anything ever gets written to it.

Here the speed of release becomes the crucial clue. Structural change in tissue — actual remodeling — takes days to weeks. [A change that completes in five seconds, mid-exhale, must be a change of maintained state, not of structure]{claim=VASO-C011}: something the body is actively doing and can stop doing. Scar tissue does not release on an exhale. The inference is sound; its premise — that the felt release corresponds to an objective local event at all — is precisely the thing never yet measured.

## What if blood talks back?

In 2008, the neuroscientists Christopher Moore and Rosa Cao proposed the hemo-neural hypothesis: that the coupling between neurons and blood runs both ways — that [local vascular state actively modulates what nearby neurons compute]{claim=VASO-C012}, through mundane physical channels: mechanical deformation sensed by pressure-gated ion channels, temperature, chemistry. The proposal looked exotic in 2008. It looks less so now: the Piezo mechanosensors earned a Nobel Prize in 2021, and in 2024 a study in Science demonstrated blood-pressure pulsations modulating neuronal activity through mechanosensitive channels in rats. The read path exists. And nothing in the logic is brain-specific — the periphery has the same ingredients, sometimes in stronger form: dorsal root ganglia wrapped in capillaries behind a leaky blood barrier, sensory endings literally wrapped around the vessels whose diameter they would be sensing.

## The synthesis, and what it explains

The researcher Michael Edward Johnson has assembled these pieces into a hypothesis he calls vasocomputation — and here the argument moves onto its speculative upper floors. Neural activity writes to the vasculature (established coupling). The vasculature can store what is written, via the latch (established physiology, speculatively applied). The stored state reads back onto neural function (the hemo-neural path). Write, store, read: [vascular tension as a memory medium participating in mental life — with the grasping that Buddhism calls tanha as its felt signature]{claim=VASO-C021}.

Whatever the fate of that identification, consider what the stack offers the humble muscle knot. [A knot becomes a latched arteriole throttling its own neighborhood — chronic local ischemia at near-zero energetic cost, producing exactly the acidic, sensitized milieu the microdialysis found, wrapped in secondary skeletal-muscle guarding]{claim=VASO-C020}. This would patch the oldest hole in trigger-point theory: the classic "energy crisis" model needed fibers in permanent maximal contraction, a metabolic bonfire nobody could explain, where a latch holds for almost nothing. It would explain why knots feel like autonomous objects, why they survive years, why the Doppler literature keeps finding flow behaving as if something upstream were clenched. And it would explain the two-key protocol: smooth muscle takes no voluntary commands, but it answers to autonomic state, and [a slow exhale is the most direct voluntary lever on that state — the one bodily rhythm that is both willed and automatic]{claim=VASO-C013}. Pressure perturbs the local loop; breath shifts the chemistry that governs unlatching. The roller is the read head; the exhale is the write head.

## The conventional account, taken seriously

Every one of those explananda has a soberer candidate explanation, and honesty requires displaying it at full strength. Tender points may be neuromuscular guarding: sustained low-level motor drive — the EMG chatter is, after all, skeletal-muscle electrophysiology by every published interpretation. The felt release may be expectation and attention doing what expectation and attention demonstrably do, riding on the genuine but global parasympathetic shift of slow breathing. The critical research report commissioned for this case graded the two linchpin propositions — that a knot objectively releases in seconds on an exhale, and that the releasing element is vascular smooth muscle — grade D: no direct evidence located, in either direction. No study has ever identified a smooth-muscle latch at a tender point. The mechanism is borrowed from vascular physiology, not yet observed in the tissue it is supposed to explain.

## The oldest anatomy text

{plate:IMG-VASO-P01}

Essentially every contemplative tradition that mapped the inner body arrived independently at the same three claims: there are knots, breath is the tool, and untying them changes consciousness. Tibetan tantric physiology describes channel-knots — rtsa mdud — constricting the flow of wind, untied by breath practice; Hindu yoga names the granthis; seventh-century Chinese medicine documented ashi points, tender spots named for the patient's cry. The standard modern move is to file this as metaphor. The alternative reading is that [millennia of practitioners with extraordinarily trained interoception were producing first-person cartography of the vascular-autonomic tension system]{claim=VASO-C022} — channels as vasculature, winds as autonomic state, knots as latches. It is at least suggestive that the traditional maps place the important knots along the torso's midline, where the sympathetic chains and dorsal root ganglia actually live. But suggestive is all it currently is: no one has ever coded the traditional locations under blinded rules and tested the alignment against chance, and until someone does, the convergence remains vulnerable to post-hoc matching. The traditions also preserved a warning this case records without endorsing a mechanism: releasing held material faster than the system can integrate is genuinely destabilizing, and the modern literature on meditation's adverse effects says the same.

## The crux

Strip everything away and the disagreement is narrower than either camp admits. Both sides accept the latch as physiology. Both sides accept that slow breathing shifts autonomic state globally. Both sides accept that people feel releases. The whole dispute funnels into one empirical question: when a knot "releases" on a slow exhale, does anything objective happen locally — a stiffness drop, a perfusion rise, time-locked to the breath, exceeding pressure, expectation, and generalized relaxation? If yes, the state-not-structure argument engages and the conventional account owes an explanation of what just changed. If no, the featured hypothesis loses its anchor phenomenon and the knot returns to the guarding-and-interpretation account, where the skeptics have been waiting.

That experiment — elastography and Doppler over a palpated knot, calibrated pressure, factorial controls, a button press at each felt release — would cost less than a mid-size grant and has never been run. Everything above the bottom rung of this case is waiting on it.

## What would settle it

This case does not end in a verdict, because on the present record no honest verdict is available. It ends in a research agenda: six funded project designs, from the keystone release-imaging study through the knot census nobody has ever taken — there is no graph of knot burden versus age, anywhere, for a phenomenon millions of people can locate in thirty seconds — to the decisive animal experiment separating vascular memory from vascular plumbing, and the unglamorous scholarship that would test whether the contemplative maps are empirical documents. The machines exist. The practitioners exist. The experiments are small, cheap, and specified below, with what each would tell us in either direction.

Someone should count. Either way, the knots are there. Press into one, and breathe out slowly.
