[p. 1]
Knots of Existence and Vasocomputation
Muscle knots, breath, and a theory connecting tension in the tissue to the structure of t
mind. Generated by Kimi and Fable.
EUGENE
AUG 13, 2026
1 Share
Text Generated fully by Kimi and Fable.
There is a strange gap at the center of musculoskeletal medicine. Anyone with a foa
roller and twenty minutes can locate dozens of small, discrete, exquisitely tender
points in their own body — most densely around the hips and shoulders, more
numerous with every passing decade. Roll across one and it announces itself
unmistakably. Yet open the research literature and you will find scientists arguing
about whether these points exist at all.
2

[p. 2]
This article is about that gap — and about a chain of ideas, running from classical
muscle physiology through a radical hypothesis about blood and thought, all the wa
to Tibetan contemplative anatomy, that may explain what these knots actually are. T
chain starts on solid experimental ground and climbs into open speculation. The ru
will be labeled along the way.
The standard name for the tender point is the “myofascial trigger point”: a
hypothesized patch of muscle stuck in micro-contraction, choking its own blood
supply, accumulating metabolites, becoming sensitive. The concept has been clinica
influential for decades and academically embattled for almost as long. Critics charg
that the construct is circular — therapists find trigger points because they are train
to find trigger points — that agreement between examiners is poor, and that imagin
has never produced a definitive picture of what a trigger point is.
Notice, however, what the critics do not dispute: that palpable, tender, precisely
localizable spots exist. The entire fight is about mechanism. And part of the reason
fight has run so long is structural. Modern medicine is organized by organ system:
orthopedics owns bones, neurology owns nerves, rheumatology owns inflammation
cardiology owns the pipes. Nobody owns muscle tone — the continuous, neurally-s
background contraction of soft tissue. No specialty means no billing codes, no
imaging protocols, no funding lines, no datasets. The skeptics’ strongest argument
“there is no evidence” — is quietly circular: there is no evidence because no one has
ever been paid to look properly.
Meanwhile, practitioners who work with these spots daily report a consistent set of
features that any candidate mechanism must explain.
First, the quality of the obstruction is distinctive. A tight muscle produces a sharp p
at the end of its stretch. A knot produces something different — a dull blockage, a
A phenomenon without a mechanism

[p. 3]
refusal to move, as though the tissue layers themselves have stopped sliding. This is
more diagnostic than it sounds: stretch pain reports through fast, myelinated,
precisely-mapped nerve fibers, while the dull, diffuse, deep ache of a knot is the
signature of visceral interoceptive channels — evolutionarily ancient, unmyelinated,
dull by design. The phenomenology is telling us that the thing under the roller is no
the muscle the roller is pressing.
Second, knots accumulate with age and correlate with declining flexibility, particul
around the hips; sustained work on them can restore range of motion that seemed
permanently lost. Fresh knots and old knots behave differently — the fresh ones yie
in a session, the ancient ones take months, as though a signal gradually became a
structure.
Third, and most strangely: pressure locates the knots, but pressure alone does not
seem to release them. Release comes with breath. Press into a knot, breathe slowly,
and on a long exhale something lets go — in seconds. Whatever a knot is, a good
theory has to explain why the exhale is the key.
A newer line of research supplies part of the picture. Fascia scientists — Carla Stec
group in Padua prominent among them — distinguish densification , where the
hyaluronan lubricant between fascial sheets becomes viscous and gluey so the layer
stop gliding, from true structural scarring. Densification is reversible with pressure
movement, and warmth, and it demonstrably increases with age as tissue dehydrate
and collagen cross-links. “Layers that will not glide” is a strikingly good description
the dull-blockage sensation. And the microdialysis work is real: Jay Shah’s group at
NIH sampled the fluid at active trigger points and found a genuinely nasty broth —
markedly acidic, loaded with substance P, CGRP, bradykinin, inflammatory cytokin
Something is there, and it is chemically angry. But neither densification nor chemis
can explain the speed of a breath-triggered release. For that, the timescale itself is t
crucial clue.

[p. 4]
Structural change in tissue — actual remodeling — takes days to weeks. A knot can
go in five seconds, mid-exhale. Whatever releases in that moment must therefore be
state rather than a structure : something the body is actively doing and can stop doing
quickly.
The nervous system is the natural suspect. Muscle tone is not a local property of
muscle; it is continuously set by neural drive. And the evidence that these spots are
under direct autonomic control has existed for decades, largely unread: needle-EMG
studies found that trigger points show spontaneous electrical chatter that rises when
subject is given a mental stressor and falls during relaxation . Read that again. You can m
a knot angrier by handing someone a math test. The brain is holding the switch. Th
is discussed more below.
A slow exhale is the most direct voluntary lever a person has on that switch.
Exhalation shifts autonomic balance toward the parasympathetic side and lowers
resting tone throughout the body — and breathing is the only bodily rhythm that is
both willed and automatic, the single voluntary handle on the entire autonomic
system. This matters more than it seems, because “just relax” is useless advice: the
somatic educator Thomas Hanna gave the reason a name, sensory-motor amnesia . Yo
cannot voluntarily release what you can no longer feel, and chronic guarding erases
exactly that feeling — Moseley’s group has shown that in chronic pain, the sensory-
cortex map of the affected region gets smudged , degraded, blurry. A knot is an
interoceptive blind spot. Its dullness is the phenomenology of neglect; the pain whe
the roller finds it is the region coming back online.
Fascia, meanwhile, has turned out to be one of the most richly innervated tissues in
the body — less a passive wrapper than a sensory organ, dense with endings that
report pressure and stretch.
The speed of release points at the nervous system

[p. 5]
This yields a first-pass model of the foam rolling protocol: the pressure is the addre
and the breath is the permission. The roller surfaces a guarded spot into awarenes
an attention cursor, re-inscribing a blurred region of the body map — and the exhal
the nervous system deciding, at that address, that it is safe to stop guarding. On this
reading, a knot is partly a stored protective decision — which would explain why it
vanish in seconds rather than the weeks that tissue repair requires. The anatomy ev
delivers a punchline: the diaphragm’s fascia is continuous with the psoas at T12–L1
and the pelvic floor moves with the breath cycle. The psoas is unreachable by any
external tool. Breath is an internal massage that reaches muscles no roller can touch
which may be why hip work, of all work, responds to it.
That model is plausible as far as it goes. But there is a deeper mechanism available,
one that lives not in the muscle a person can flex, but in the muscle they cannot.
The speed-of-release argument says a knot must be a state, not a structure. The
evidence that these spots are under autonomic control has existed for decades, large
unread outside a small clinical literature. In 1993, Hubbard and Berkoff inserted fin
needle electrodes into trigger points in the trapezius and recorded continuous
spontaneous electrical activity — ongoing chatter in muscle that was supposedly at
rest. Move the needle roughly a centimeter into non-tender muscle of the same
trapezius and the signal vanishes. The knot is not merely stiffer and more tender th
its surroundings; it is a small island of maintained electrical activity.
The follow-up, from McNulty, Gevirtz and colleagues in 1994, is the remarkable one
With electrodes in place, they gave subjects a psychological stressor — mental
arithmetic. Activity at the trigger point rose. Activity at a control site a short distan
away, in the same muscle, did not, and the subject was not generally tensing. A pure
mental event, involving no movement, selectively turned up the electrical activity
inside one tender point. Later work from the same lineage showed the reverse —
Two experiments that catch the loop in motion

[p. 6]
relaxation training lowering trigger point activity — and, most tellingly, that infusin
the site with phentolamine, a drug that blocks sympathetic signaling, substantially
quieted it. Interpretations of what the chatter is remain contested (dysfunctional
endplates, overactive muscle spindles), and the studies are small and old. But under
every reading, the finding survives: a discrete tender spot maintained by ongoing
neural activity, dialed up by stress and down by relaxation and sympathetic blockad
The brain has the knot’s address.
If that is the writing half of the loop, a 2026 study in Nature Human Behaviour suppli
its regulatory counterpart. Mizrachi and colleagues induced identical acute
inflammation in the same participants twice — a standardized histamine skin prick
manipulating only where attention went: toward the sensations at the inflamed site
away toward distractors. Internal attention produced roughly 1.5-fold smaller and
faster-resolving responses, in about 90% of participants, replicated in a second
experiment where the visual input and cognitive demands were matched exactly, so
that the direction of attention was the only variable. Sympathetic arousal cannot
explain it: skin conductance, heart rate, skin temperature and self-reported anxiety
were statistically identical across conditions, while heart rate variability — an index
vagal tone — was significantly higher under internal attention. Two separable
channels emerged. A sensory route: numbing the site with lidocaine specifically
degraded the response’s resolution , the decline back toward baseline. And a top-dow
route that survived the anesthetic — vagal engagement and inflammatory regulatio
persisted even when peripheral sensation was pharmacologically blunted.
The measured tissue in that study was, not incidentally, a vascular bed. The flare is
arteriolar smooth muscle relaxing; the wheal is plasma escaping through gaps that
open when endothelial cells retract — a retraction driven by myosin light chain
phosphorylation, the same kinase-phosphatase switch that governs the latch, runni
one cell layer over. What the study establishes is not that attention grips or releases
vessels directly; the demonstrated route runs through the vagal anti-inflammatory
reflex over twenty minutes, and the authors are careful to note that the

[p. 7]
parasympathetic system does not innervate skin directly. What it establishes is the
existence and direction of the channel: voluntary interoceptive attention, with no
change whatever in arousal, measurably regulating peripheral vascular behavior in
ordinary people, with effect sizes most drug trials would envy.
Put the two studies side by side and the loop closes. Cognition can write tension int
specific peripheral site; attention and its autonomic train can regulate it back down
And the authors’ own closing caution reads like the ledger’s origin story: they obser
that turning attention away from unpleasant bodily sensations is a common habit a
even a clinical practice, that this may carry a physiological cost, and that habitual
avoidance of symptoms could contribute to the persistence of conditions like chron
pain. A lifetime of exteroceptive living is a lifetime of unregulated periphery —
plausibly the conditions under which holdings accumulate.
Which raises the question of what, physically, does the holding. There is a mechani
available, and it lives not in the muscle a person can flex, but in the muscle they
cannot.
The latch-bridge: a ratchet made of meat

[p. 8]


[p. 9]
The body contains a second muscular system under no direct voluntary control:
smooth muscle, lining the blood vessels, gut, and airways. Smooth muscle has a
property that skeletal muscle lacks, textbook physiology since Hai and Murphy
formalized it in 1988: the latch-bridge state .
Skeletal muscle is expensive. Every second a bicep holds a weight, molecular motor
are cycling and burning fuel; stop paying and the muscle drops. Smooth muscle solv
a different engineering problem. Arteries must hold partial contraction — tone —
continuously, for a lifetime; doing so with continuously cycling motors would be
metabolically ruinous. So smooth muscle evolved a ratchet. Under the right chemic
conditions, its molecular motors grip and then lock , holding tension at a small fract
of the energetic cost, for minutes, hours, or in some tissues essentially indefinitely.
The activating signal can disappear entirely and the grip remains. The founding
laboratory observation is exactly this dissociation: stimulate an artery and the
chemical activation spikes and then falls back toward baseline, while the force simp
stays.
Three features of the latch matter here. It is a kinetic trap , not damage — latched tis
looks normal under a microscope; it is just holding. It is remote-controlled by the
autonomic nervous system: stress chemistry makes latches form more easily and sti
harder, while the body’s relaxation pathways (the nitric oxide cascade among them)
actively pick the locks. And it exhibits hysteresis — the tissue’s present state depend
on its history, not merely its current inputs. Two identical vessels receiving identica
signals can be in different states depending on what happened to them an hour ago
That last property has a name in engineering. A cheap, history-dependent hold that
persists after its input vanishes is a memory element. Biology ships a one-bit storag
device, distributed through every vascularized tissue in the body. The question is
whether anything ever gets written to it.

[p. 10]
In 2008, neuroscientists Christopher Moore and Rosalind Cao proposed what they
called the hemo-neural hypothesis. The background is uncontroversial: neural activ
drives local blood flow — this coupling is what fMRI measures. The universal
assumption has been that the traffic runs one way. Blood is the caterer, delivering fu
where the work happens, with no opinions about the computation.
Moore and Cao proposed that the arrow runs both ways: that local vascular state
actively modulates what nearby neurons compute. The candidate channels are
mundane and physical. Vessels dilating and constricting mechanically deform the
surrounding tissue, and neurons carry pressure-sensitive ion channels — the Piezo
channels, whose discovery earned the 2021 Nobel Prize and made this proposal
considerably less exotic than it sounded in 2008. Blood flow changes local temperat
to which channel kinetics are sensitive, and washes signaling molecules such as nit
oxide through the tissue. Astrocytes physically bridge vessels and synapses, position
to translate the state of one into the behavior of the other. The hypothesis remains a
minority position, but the evidence has drifted toward it rather than away — and it
carries a delicious irony. If it is right, decades of brain imaging have been watching
blood on the assumption that it was a proxy for mind, when the blood may have bee
part of the mind all along.
Crucially, nothing in the logic is brain-specific. The periphery has all the same
ingredients, sometimes in stronger form. The gut’s intrinsic nervous system contain
on the order of half a billion neurons embedded in intensely vascular tissue. The do
root ganglia — the nodes beside the spine housing the cell bodies of every sensory
neuron serving the body — are dense clusters of nerve cells wrapped in capillaries,
unlike the brain they sit behind a leaky blood barrier, directly exposed to vascular
chemistry. Peripheral sensory endings are the body’s mechanosensation specialists,
many cases literally wrapped around the vessels whose diameter changes they woul
The hemo-neural hypothesis: what if blood talks
back?

[p. 11]
be sensing. If vascular state modulates neural function anywhere, the periphery is a
least as good a venue as the cortex.
The researcher Michael Edward Johnson has assembled these pieces into a hypothe
he calls vasocomputation — and here the argument moves onto its speculative uppe
floors. The lower floors are established physiology; this floor is a proposal.
The synthesis runs as follows. Neural activity writes to the vasculature (established:
neurovascular coupling). The vasculature can store what is written, via the latch
(established physiology, speculatively applied). The stored vascular state reads back
onto neural function (the hemo-neural hypothesis). Write, store, read: together they
form a loop — a circuit whose activity constricts its own vessels, whose constriction
biases its own activity. A self-sustaining grip.
Vasocomputation: the stack assembled
Michael Edward Johnson
@ johnsonmxe
Last year I proposed “vasocomputation,” that vascular tension acts as a
special type of memory that regulates neural dynamic range. Recently at
@JoinEdgeCity I shared some updates: how ‘thoughts ʼ are patterns of
vascular tension, and implications for Buddhist enlightenment
1/x
6:45 AM · Dec 2, 2024 · 234K Views
40 Replies · 111 Reposts · 1.02K Likes
0:00

[p. 12]
Johnson’s boldest move is to identify this grip with something specific in the
phenomenology of mind: clinging. In his framing, when the mind holds a prediction
rigid — refuses to update an expectation, grasps at how things should be — one
physical implementation is vascular smooth muscle latching around the relevant
tissue. Tension as a pause button on inference. Buddhism has a technical term for
precisely this mental motion: tanha , craving, the grasping the tradition identifies as
the root of suffering. On the vasocomputation view, clinging is not like a grip. It is o
Whatever the fate of that identification, consider what the stack offers the humble
muscle knot. A knot becomes a self-contained loop in the periphery: latched
microvessels in the fascia sitting against the nerve endings embedded in that same
fascia, each sustaining the other — a small computational cyst that persists without
the brain’s ongoing permission. This would explain why knots feel like autonomous
objects with definite locations. Why they survive years of ordinary life. Why they
accumulate — every unresolved stress leaving a small held tension, the body becom
a ledger of everything never quite let go.
It also patches the oldest hole in trigger-point theory. The classic “energy crisis”
hypothesis required fibers in maximal contraction, burning enormous ATP; a body
carrying a field of them would be a metabolic bonfire no one could explain. The latc
dissolves the problem: a latched arteriole upstream creates chronic local ischemia a
near-zero energetic cost, producing exactly the hypoxic, acidic milieu Shah’s
microdialysis found — the broth that sensitizes the local nociceptors and generates
the dull ache. The knot becomes a two-layer object: a smooth-muscle latch throttlin
supply, plus whatever skeletal fibers secondarily guard the region.
And above all, the stack explains the two-key protocol. Smooth muscle cannot be
commanded voluntarily, but it responds exquisitely to autonomic state — and the
exhale is the master key to that state. Pressure perturbs the local loop; breath shifts
global chemistry that governs unlatching. Neither alone suffices. The roller is the re
head; the exhale is the write head. Anyone who has rolled seriously knows this patte

[p. 13]
in their own tissue. A knot, in the most modern framing available, is a stale lock fil
cached “hold!” command from a war that ended decades ago, still consuming
resources, still blocking range, still issuing its order to a battle long over.
Here is a fact that should stop any curious person cold: nobody has ever counted.
There is no graph of knot burden versus age. There is no distribution map across th
body. There is no knot census — not a small one, not a bad one, none . For a
phenomenon millions of people can locate in thirty seconds, the total absence of ba
natural-history data is the actual scandal.
What should the curve look like? Reasoning from the components: near zero at birt
— infants pandiculate constantly, are famously supple, and if guarding is learned, th
have not yet accumulated the injury history and emotional bracing that writes the
knots in. Roughly monotonic accumulation through midlife, as every mechanism
The census nobody has taken

[p. 14]
points the same direction: collagen cross-linking via glycation, hyaluronan
densification, declining vagal tone, decades of the same low-threshold motor units
doing all the postural work (Hägg’s “Cinderella fibers” — first recruited, never reste
and the slow accumulation of held responses to stress and injury. The chair is a kno
factory: sustained hip flexion, inhibited glutes, loaded traps. Then, possibly, a late-l
phase transition: as muscle mass disappears after sixty, stuck tone may convert to
diffuse fibrosis — knot count might even fall in the elderly while stiffness rises, the
knots calcifying into the wallpaper.
The distribution should be pure engineering: stress concentrators and startle muscl
The junction zones — cervicothoracic, thoracolumbar, lumbosacral, hip. The anti-
gravity chain. The brace muscles: jaw, throat, diaphragm, belly, pelvic floor.
And the latch model adds a sly twist: one version of this curve has already been
measured. Vascular medicine has been graphing vasomotor latch burden against ag
for decades — it is called arterial stiffening, tracked by pulse wave velocity, rising
relentlessly from the twenties onward. Cardiology files this as a plumbing problem.
The vasocomputation reading says it is a memory problem: decades of cached defen
setpoints written into vessel walls. The knot-by-age curve may be sitting in the
literature already, under a different name.
One more arithmetic worth savoring. Deep practitioners sometimes estimate their
knot counts in the hundreds of thousands, which sounds like hyperbole — until you
learn that the human body runs on the order of a few hundred thousand motor units .
a small knot is a stuck motor unit, a fiber-segment contracture at an endplate zone,
a latched microvessel, the estimate is anatomically plausible. A skilled roller may be
feeling, literally, the granularity of the motor system, unit by unit. Nobody has ever
made that arithmetic explicit, because nobody has ever counted.
The scanner question

[p. 15]
The obvious retort to “nobody has ever counted” is: hasn’t anyone looked ? Yes — an
the results are encouraging, disappointing, and clarifying at once. Encouraging:
several modalities already detect trigger points reliably, and as of mid-2026 a whole
body scanner exists that could perform the census. Disappointing: nobody has aime
any of it at count, distribution, or age. Clarifying: which modalities work, and which
return nulls, tells us what a knot is.
If latched tension is real, it should be mappable, because everything a latch does ca
a shadow some existing scanner can catch : restricted blood flow (Doppler), held
stiffness (elastography), slowly changing composition (density imaging), and — the
subtle one — a metabolic cold spot , since the latch’s entire purpose is holding tension
without burning fuel (metabolic imaging). The question is which shadow is sharpes
Ultrasound is the decisive winner. Modern machines measure stiffness (shear-wave
elastography) and small-vessel flow (sensitive Doppler) through the same probe , at kno
depths, at frame rates fast enough to watch a release happen, radiation-free. And
Doppler has quietly produced the most consistent positive results in the whole
imaging literature: active trigger points show abnormal local hemodynamics — hig
prevalence of retrograde flow , elevated pulsatility index , and velocities that separat
active from latent points. Through the latch lens this is almost on-the-nose: a knot’
signature is a vascular bed behaving abnormally — flow reversed, resistance elevat
as if something upstream were clenched. The literature stumbled onto the latch’s
footprint without knowing what it was looking at.
The coverage problem just got solved — by an unexpected donor. Ultrasound’s
historic limit was coverage: a postage stamp at a time. In June 2026, Midjourney —
AI image company — announced a full-body “ultrasonic CT”: a 70 cm ring of ~358,0
transducers (ultrasound-on-chip technology licensed from Butterfly Network) aroun
a shallow pool, reconstructing a sub-millimeter 3D body map in about sixty seconds
no magnets, no radiation — with claimed speeds and costs orders of magnitude
beyond MRI, spa-scale deployment plans, and a stated goal of 50,000 scanners by 20

[p. 16]
One gap matters enormously: as announced, it images composition, not state — th
sediment layer, not the grip. But the gap is bridgeable: the ring’s substrate is the sam
hardware class that performs elastography and Doppler elsewhere — a firmware
question, not new physics — and its slow-descent geometry makes a “dwell mode”
over a marked knot a software feature, not a retrofit. Its headline weakness for
screening (ultrasound can’t see past bone; MRI owns the heart) is irrelevant here:
knots live in muscle and fascia, ultrasound’s home turf. Caveats stand — unverified
multiples, no diagnostic clearance — but the strategic implication is plain: the who
body machine exists; what it lacks is the right software.
MRI is the deep-tissue play, and its nulls are informative. Conventional MRI has
largely failed to image trigger points — invisible on T1, preliminary promise on T2-
mapping. But MRI excels at structure ; a knot invisible to structural imaging yet visib
to flow imaging is exactly what state-not-structure predicts. The delicious detail:
fMRI’s BOLD signal is already a vascular measurement — neuroscience spent decades
treating blood as a proxy for neurons; on the vasocomputation view it was partly
imaging the computational medium itself. Muscle BOLD and MR elastography are
established research techniques; MRI’s weakness is a feeble resting signal — it wan
challenge paradigm.
Density imaging is the sediment layer — CT attenuation and echotexture see
structure, not state: fatty infiltration, fibrosis, thickened fascia. Useful as the atlas’s
structural base layer; the sediment marks where the river has been running.
PET is the dark horse, with a distinctive prediction. Inflamed tissue lights up on
FDG-PET; a latch should do the opposite — stiff on elastography, electrically activ
on EMG, metabolically cold . That triple signature belongs to no conventional lesio
finding it would be strong evidence the tissue is doing something current taxonomi
don’t describe. Radiation rules PET out for censuses, but one small overlay study at
palpated knots could establish the signature — and there’s precedent for whole-bod

[p. 17]
metabolic imaging revealing overlooked physiology: routine PET is how active brow
fat was discovered in adults, hiding in plain sight in thousands of oncology scans.
The upgrade that applies to every modality: the provocation map. A static map sho
where tension sits; Johnson’s phrase — a map of “where you can clench” — implies
better. Image at rest, then during a mental stressor, then during breath work, and
subtract: the difference map is a functional atlas of each person’s clench repertoire
the same task-contrast logic by which fMRI transformed brain science. We already
know from the needle studies that the brain can write to a knot on command. Nobo
has ever watched it happen on a scanner.
So what can we currently surmise? Three fragments, none collected with this
question in mind. First : rheumatology’s fibromyalgia-era 18-site tender-point exam,
applied to community samples, reads like a proto-census — tender points nearly
universal (medians 6 in women, 3 in men), counts tracking distress and poor sleep rath
than tissue damage, distributed continuously across the population. Collected to
adjudicate a diagnosis and then abandoned — the closest thing to a knot-count curv
science possesses, with exactly the correlate a stored-tension account predicts. Seco

if the exotic upper floors collapse, the lower floors pay for themselves — a validated
release protocol, an age-stratified atlas of human tension, and a whole-body stiffnes
scanner would each matter for ordinary pain medicine, sports science, and healthy
aging. The downside is a useful contribution to musculoskeletal science. And if the
upper floors hold, the implications compound quickly: the foam roller in the closet
becomes a crude single-pixel probe of the layer where body and mind transact; the
traditions that spoke of untying the knots of existence turn out to have been writing
engineering documentation; and the most interesting organ system of the coming
decades is one medicine has been imaging for twenty-five years while calling it nois
The body, on this view, is not a machine that wears out. It is a ledger — a record of
every threat ever met with holding, written in vasomotor tone and fascial
densification, accumulating decade over decade, silently consuming range of motio
attention, and something harder to name. The experiment is buildable. The
practitioners exist. The scanner physics is solved. The only thing missing is that
nobody has ever bothered to count.
The wager

[p. 34]
Someone should count.
Either way, the knots are there. Press into one, and breathe out slowly.

Knots, Vasocomputation, and the Biology of
Stored Tension: A Critical Research Report
Executive summary
The uploaded essay, Knots of Existence and Vasocomputation , proposes an unusually ambitious synthesis:
myofascial “knots” are interpreted as persistent physiological states; vascular smooth-muscle latch states
are proposed as a low-energy storage mechanism; vascular state is then hypothesized to feed back onto
neural computation; and Michael Edward Johnson's “vasocomputation” framework is used to connect this
loop to predictive processing, trauma, contemplative “knots,” and ultimately consciousness. The essay
explicitly acknowledges that this chain begins with established physiology and becomes increasingly
speculative; it also states that its text was generated by Kimi and Fable.  filecite  turn0file0 
The central conclusion of this review is that several lower-level components of the essay are individually
real and scientifically important, but the proposed integration has not yet been demonstrated . In
particular:
Mathematical knot theory is highly developed and genuinely useful in biology , especially for
circular DNA, topoisomerases, viral DNA packing, and knotted proteins. Type-II topoisomerases
actively simplify DNA knotting below thermal-equilibrium levels, and confinement inside viral capsids
generates measurable knot spectra. There is, however, no evidence that a clinical “muscle
knot” is a topological knot in the mathematical sense . The word knot currently connects these
literatures metaphorically, not mechanistically.
Myofascial trigger points have measurable correlates , including altered local electrophysiology,
chemistry, stiffness, and hemodynamics. Hubbard and Berkoff reported spontaneous needle-EMG
activity localized to trigger-point loci; McNulty and colleagues found that mental arithmetic
selectively increased activity at trigger points; Shah and colleagues found acidic and mediator-rich
biochemical environments; and an imaging systematic review concluded that active and latent
trigger points can exhibit quantifiable biomechanical and blood-flow differences. However,
trigger-point identification by palpation has historically shown limited inter-examiner reliability, and
the underlying entity and mechanism remain controversial.
The smooth-muscle “latch” phenomenon is established physiology. Hai and Murphy's kinetic
model accounts for force maintenance with reduced cross-bridge cycling after myosin
dephosphorylation. But treating this contractile state as a literal long-duration information register—
especially one capable of storing semantic predictions, trauma, or “clinging”—is an extrapolation, not
a result of the latch literature.
Bidirectional vascular–neural interaction is more scientifically plausible than it was when
Moore and Cao proposed the hemo-neural hypothesis in 2008. Their hypothesis argued that
hemodynamic variables might participate in information processing rather than merely supporting

neuronal metabolism. Subsequent work has shown active neurovascular signaling through capillary
endothelium and, particularly strikingly, a 2024 Science study demonstrated that arterial pressure
pulsations can modulate neuronal activity through mechanosensitive ion channels in rats. This
supports the general proposition vascular state → neural effect . It does not establish the much
stronger proposition vascular latch state = cognitive memory or predictive prior .
The “Michael Johnson” relevant here is Michael Edward Johnson , who describes himself as a
philosopher and neuroscientist and lists Vasocomputation among his major theoretical projects. His
2023–2025 OpenTheory essay proposes the “Compressive Vasomotion,” “Vascular Clamp,” and
“Latched Hyperprior” hypotheses, explicitly mapping vascular smooth-muscle contraction onto
prediction, medium-term memory, and Buddhist tanhā/upādāna . Based on the literature located
for this review, Johnson's vasocomputation work remains a theoretical/self-published research
program rather than an experimentally validated, peer-reviewed theory . Current 2026 Edge City
materials describe experiments intended to seek direct evidence, rather than already-established
results.
A particularly important neighboring literature actually demonstrates something structurally
reminiscent of vasocomputation: Physarum slime mold stores information in the geometry of a
living flow network. Kramar and Alim experimentally showed that nutrient locations become
encoded in a hierarchy of tube diameters, which subsequently biases transport and behavior.
This is one of the strongest empirical precedents for the general idea that the state of a biological
transport network can encode history and influence subsequent behavior . It is not evidence
that mammalian arteries do the same for thoughts.
The uploaded essay's strongest untested claim is therefore not that blood vessels affect nerves—
they do—but that a spatially localized, history-dependent vascular state can store behaviorally
meaningful information and subsequently bias nearby neural computation after the initiating
signal disappears . That claim is experimentally accessible and should be treated as the core
vasocomputation hypothesis.
The essay's proposed “breath-release” mechanism is currently far ahead of the data. Slow breathing
reproducibly alters cardiovascular autonomic indices such as heart-rate variability, but this does not
establish that an exhale rapidly unlatches a specific arteriole at an identified trigger point. The
crucial experiment—simultaneous high-speed measurement of local stiffness, perfusion, respiration,
EMG and subjective release—appears not yet to have been performed.
A major 2026 development deserves particular attention. Mizrachi, Rottem and Rozenkrantz
reported in Nature Human Behaviour that voluntarily directing attention to an experimentally
inflamed site reduced subsequent histamine-induced inflammatory responses in preregistered
within-subject experiments. The study provides unusually strong human evidence for top-down
modulation of peripheral physiology, while its authors explicitly note that the molecular/cellular
mediators were not directly measured and that extrapolation to chronic disease is uncertain.
This is relevant to vasocomputation because it establishes a controllable cognition-to-periphery
channel; it does not establish a vascular latch mechanism.
Overall evidence judgment: the essay is most valuable as a research-generating synthesis . Its lower floors—
trigger-point physiology, autonomic modulation, smooth-muscle latch kinetics, neurovascular coupling and

patterns, contemplative knots as first-person maps of these latches, and enlightenment as systematic

Conceptual, historical, and mathematical foundations
Three meanings of “knot” must be kept separate
The most important conceptual discipline for this subject is to avoid silently moving between three different
senses of knot .
A topological knot is, classically, an embedding of a circle into three-dimensional space—usually or
—considered up to ambient isotopy. Two diagrams representing the same tame knot can be
transformed into one another through planar deformation plus the three Reidemeister moves. Knot
invariants assign quantities that remain unchanged under such equivalences; familiar examples include the
fundamental group of the complement, Alexander polynomial and Jones polynomial.
A molecular knot is a physical polymer configuration that can meaningfully be classified using these ideas.
Circular DNA is especially clean mathematically because it is already a closed curve. Protein backbones are
open chains, so a closure convention or another operational definition is required; Taylor's seminal
computational study explicitly confronted this issue when identifying deeply knotted proteins.
A myofascial “knot” or trigger point is a clinical/palpatory construct referring to a localized tender or
mechanically abnormal region. Nothing in the present trigger-point literature demonstrates that tissue
fibers there constitute a nontrivial topological embedding. The uploaded essay's “knot” is therefore not
currently a knot-theoretic object .
This distinction matters because otherwise the rigor of mathematical knot theory can accidentally lend
authority to a physiological hypothesis with which it has, so far, no demonstrated topological connection.

Historical trajectory
The timeline combines several otherwise separate research traditions: mathematical topology, molecular
topology, smooth-muscle physiology, trigger-point research, adaptive biological networks, neurovascular
neuroscience and Johnson's theoretical synthesis.

DNA is the strongest bridge between knot theory and biology
DNA topology provides perhaps the clearest example of a topological variable carrying functional biological
consequences. Type-II topoisomerases transiently pass one DNA duplex through another, changing
knotting and catenation. Rybenkov, Ullsperger, Vologodskii and Cozzarelli found that these enzymes drive
knot and catenane fractions as much as approximately 80-fold below equilibrium values, demonstrating
active control of a global topological property rather than passive equilibration.

explored how geometrical selection or kinetic proofreading can permit such topology simplification.
Viral DNA provides another striking experimental case. Arsuaga and colleagues found very high knotting
probability in DNA extracted from tailless P4 bacteriophage capsids; Monte Carlo polymer simulations
reproduced the tendency of confinement to generate highly knotted molecules. Later analysis of the knot
spectrum revealed information about the chiral organization of DNA inside capsids. Here, knot
statistics function as an indirect probe of otherwise inaccessible three-dimensional biological
organization .
This is a legitimate precedent for using topology as an informational observable—but it is categorically
different from calling a tender muscular region a knot.
Proteins show that topology can constrain biological dynamics
Taylor's 2000 Nature study developed an orientation-independent computational method for locating knots
in open protein chains and identified a deep figure-eight knot in acetohydroxy acid isomeroreductase.
Subsequent protein-knot research has examined how topological entanglement affects folding, mechanical
stability, enzymatic architecture and degradation.
Thus real biological knots can influence kinetics and function. The correct inference is modest but
important: topological state can be biologically consequential . It does not imply that all persistent
biological states called “knots” are topological.

For the vasocomputation question, the slime mold Physarum polycephalum may be more relevant than
molecular knotting.

locations by short routes through a maze. Tero, Kobayashi and Nakagaki subsequently modeled its
adaptive network with flow-dependent conductance: tubes carrying greater flux thicken and poorly used
tubes regress. In simplified form,

optimization without a central controller. Tero and colleagues later showed experimentally and
computationally that Physarum networks make trade-offs between transport efficiency, construction cost
and fault tolerance comparable to engineered transportation networks.

Kramar and Alim's 2021 study moves still closer to Johnson's intuition. They observed a local nutrient
stimulus changing tube-wall properties and producing network-wide redistribution of tube diameters. The
altered hierarchy persisted after the immediate stimulus and biased later migration. Their experimental
observations plus model led them to describe the tube-diameter hierarchy as a form of memory.
The architecture is remarkably suggestive:
This is an empirically demonstrated write–store–read loop in a living flow network .
It strengthens the general scientific plausibility of morphology- or conductance-based biological memory.
However, there are decisive differences from mammalian vasculature. Physarum's tubes constitute the
organism's own motile transport body, and their remodeling occurs through a specialized cytoskeletal/flow
system. Mammalian blood vessels are embedded within a highly differentiated organism whose neural,
endothelial, metabolic, endocrine and mechanical controls are much more complex. Therefore, Physarum
should be treated as a proof of principle for biological flow-network memory , not evidence for human
vasocomputation.
Neurovascular signaling is genuinely bidirectional
The classical textbook picture in which neural activity controls blood flow is now known to be only part of
neurovascular biology. Longden and colleagues demonstrated that brain capillary endothelial cells sense
extracellular potassium associated with neural activity and propagate electrical signals upstream to dilate
arterioles—a mechanism by which the vascular network actively detects local neural demand.
Moore and Cao's 2008 hemo-neural hypothesis went a step further, proposing that blood-flow variables
could directly alter neuronal computation through mechanical, thermal, chemical or other pathways.
A particularly relevant advance came in 2024: Salameh and colleagues reported in Science that physiological
blood-pressure pulsations influenced neuronal activity in rat brain tissue and awake animals through
mechanosensitive ion-channel mechanisms, with effects occurring on rapid timescales. This is genuine
evidence for the causal direction
The scientific gap is therefore narrower than “blood cannot possibly compute.” The real unresolved
question is what information vascular variables carry, how long it persists, whether it is locally
addressable, and whether manipulating that stored vascular state changes cognition in an
information-specific way .

The vasocomputation author is Michael Edward Johnson . His OpenTheory biography describes his work as

Johnson's three central hypotheses
Johnson's Principles of Vasocomputation states three especially concrete proposals.
The Compressive Vasomotion Hypothesis proposes that rhythmic vasomotion could operate as a
changing mechanical compression field that affects nearby neural resonances.
The Vascular Clamp Hypothesis proposes that vascular contraction can temporarily stabilize or “freeze”
nearby neural patterns or plasticity, effectively acting as medium-term memory or a prediction.
The Latched Hyperprior Hypothesis goes further: prolonged vascular smooth-muscle contraction is
proposed to engage latch dynamics and thereby maintain nearby circuitry in a constrained state after the
original initiating conditions have passed. Johnson maps such persistent constraints onto “hyperpriors” in
predictive-processing language and ultimately onto Buddhist concepts of craving or clinging.
The attractive architecture is:
What is experimentally established: neural activity changes vascular state; smooth muscle can maintain
force efficiently; vascular variables can feed back onto neurons.
What is not established: that the latch stores an identifiable prediction, that it maintains a particular
neural representation, or that erasing the vascular state selectively erases or relaxes that representation.

The latch is a mechanism of force maintenance, not yet a memory register
Hai and Murphy's influential model describes smooth-muscle cross-bridge states involving phosphorylation
and dephosphorylation. During sustained contraction, force can remain comparatively high while
phosphorylation and cross-bridge cycling fall, accounting for economical tonic contraction. Reviews of
the latch-bridge hypothesis emphasize both the reality of economical sustained tension and continuing
complexity in the precise molecular interpretation.
Calling this a memory requires an additional operational criterion. In dynamical systems, any hysteretic
state can be said to contain information about history. But biological memory relevant to cognition
normally requires at least:
plus
and ideally
The latch physiology directly supports the first criterion in a limited mechanical sense. It does not by itself
establish the latter two at a cognitive level.
This is a central place where the uploaded essay's language becomes too strong. Describing vascular latch
as a “one-bit storage device distributed through every vascularized tissue” is an illuminating engineering
metaphor, but it should not be treated as an experimentally demonstrated storage architecture.

Other key proponents and adjacent research programs
Christopher Moore and Rosalind Cao are indispensable because their hemo-neural hypothesis provides
the most direct conceptual ancestor of Johnson's “read” path. Their 2008 paper explicitly asked whether
blood-flow changes may themselves alter information processing.
Karen Alim and Mirna Kramar provide the strongest experimental example of a living flow-network
architecture functioning as memory. Their Physarum work should be central to any rigorous future
vasocomputation paper, because it supplies a concrete comparator rather than a purely philosophical
analogy.
Atsushi Tero and Toshiyuki Nakagaki established much of the adaptive-flow-network framework showing
how local flow reinforcement can perform globally useful computation without centralized control.
Michael Levin and collaborators demonstrate that non-neural physiological networks can encode
persistent pattern information. Durant et al. showed that transient manipulation of endogenous bioelectric
gradients in planaria can produce altered regenerative anatomies that persist through subsequent

genetic pattern memory, but it is bioelectric/gap-junction physiology , not vascular-latch memory.
Levin's group's 2022 adult Xenopus study is similarly important but frequently overinterpreted in popular
discussions. A 24-hour wearable bioreactor intervention delivering a five-drug regenerative cocktail
produced long-lasting tissue repatterning, reinnervation and improved sensorimotor function over many
months. This demonstrates that a brief intervention can initiate a long biological developmental
program. It does not demonstrate that cognition, meditation, attention or vascular unlatching can trigger
comparable structural regeneration.
Current status of Johnson's program
As of August 2026, the sources located here indicate that Johnson's vasocomputation theory is primarily
documented through OpenTheory and related talks/projects rather than a peer-reviewed experimental
literature. Current Edge City material describes a “Vasocomputation: The Vascular Imprint of Stress and
Trauma” project associated with Michael Johnson and Alex Rockhill, including efforts to determine whether
practices such as tension/trauma release alter microvascular tension.
That distinction is important. There is a legitimate research program here, but the appropriate scholarly
wording is presently:
vasocomputation is a testable theoretical synthesis built from established vascular
physiology and emerging vascular–neural interaction data, not an experimentally
established theory of cognition.
Critical evidence audit of the “Knots of Existence” article
The uploaded article is unusually useful because it explicitly presents itself as a stack of progressively more
speculative claims. The main scholarly task is therefore not wholesale acceptance or rejection, but
identifying precisely where evidential support changes category.  filecite  turn0file0 
Myofascial trigger points: real observations, unsettled ontology
Hubbard and Berkoff's 1993 needle-EMG study reported spontaneous activity localized to tiny trigger-point
regions but absent in nearby non-tender tissue. McNulty et al. then studied 14 subjects and found that
a mental-arithmetic stressor increased EMG activity specifically at trigger-point sites while nearby control
tissue remained comparatively silent. This is genuinely intriguing evidence that local trigger-point
physiology can be influenced by psychological stress without requiring obvious whole-muscle contraction.
Yet neither experiment identifies the active structure as a blood vessel. The signal was recorded
electrophysiologically and has been interpreted in terms of motor endplates, muscle spindles or other
neuromuscular sources. Therefore, using these studies as evidence for “the brain can modulate the state
of a trigger point” is defensible; using them as evidence for “the brain writes a vascular latch” is not.
Shah et al. provided a second independent type of evidence. Using microdialysis-like sampling, they
reported that active trigger-point sites showed lower pH and increased concentrations of nociceptive/

Fascia and “densification”
Carla Stecco and colleagues have provided substantial anatomical evidence that hyaluronan is associated
with fascial interfaces and may contribute to layer gliding; they have proposed that changes in HA
aggregation or viscosity could contribute to fascial “densification.” This is a plausible mechanism for
altered sliding behavior.
However, “fascial densification” should not be treated as an established explanation for trigger points. Some
of the evidence is anatomical, cadaveric or mechanistic rather than direct prospective demonstration that a
given painful trigger point consists of reversible HA aggregation. Moreover, a quantitative study of HA
across fascial sites did not find a simple universal age effect of the kind implied by the essay's broad
statement that such densification demonstrably increases with age.

“Vascular clamp,” hypoxia and confounding
Any experiment purporting to demonstrate vasocomputational memory must distinguish an information-
bearing vascular effect from ordinary changes in oxygen, glucose, pH, temperature and waste clearance.
Moore and Cao themselves framed multiple possible hemo-neural mechanisms.
For example, if experimentally constricting a vessel suppresses nearby neural activity, that result alone is
not evidence that the vessel is “computing”: reduced perfusion can alter neuronal activity through
straightforward metabolic limitation. A convincing vasocomputation experiment must show structured
modulation beyond nonspecific ischemic suppression , ideally while oxygenation and metabolic variables
are separately measured or clamped.
The 2024 demonstration of rapid mechanosensitive effects is consequently important: it identifies one route
through which vascular mechanical state can alter neuronal behavior without requiring slow nutrient
deprivation.

The most productive way to develop vasocomputation is to remove consciousness, Buddhism and
trauma from the first generation of experiments and first determine whether the proposed physical
memory element exists. If the basic mechanism survives, the higher-level claims can then be examined.

Open questions
The field would advance most rapidly by answering a small number of well-posed questions rather than
expanding the phenomenological superstructure.
First, what is the physical object being palpated at a trigger point? Existing electrical, biochemical and
imaging signals do not yet converge on a single lesion type.
Second, does a trigger point possess a reproducible fast state transition? Without objective time-
resolved evidence, “release” remains partly dependent on subjective and practitioner reports.
Third, can smooth-muscle latch persist on the durations Johnson's theory requires? Physiological low-
energy force maintenance and cognitive memory lasting days, months or years are radically different
timescale claims.
Fourth, is neural readout of vascular state information-specific? This is the difference between vascular
modulation and vascular computation.
Fifth, what is actually stored? Vessel radius, myosin phosphorylation, endothelial state, pericyte state,
extracellular matrix mechanics, innervation, receptor expression, local metabolites and structural
remodeling can all generate history dependence. Calling all such persistence “the latch” risks collapsing
multiple biological timescales into a single mechanism.
Sixth, what distinguishes an adaptive vascular memory from pathology? A history-dependent state may
be beneficial—local autoregulatory adaptation—or harmful. A viable theory must predict the conditions
under which persistence increases versus decreases future performance.
Seventh, does the traditional contemplative literature contain anatomically falsifiable information?
That question can be studied, but only through preregistered mapping rather than retrospective
resemblance.
Epistemic conclusion
The most defensible version of the emerging picture is:
rather than
There is now excellent reason to reject an overly passive conception of vasculature. Vascular endothelial
cells sense neural-associated signals; vessels participate actively in neurovascular communication; arterial
mechanics can alter neuronal activity; living flow networks in other organisms can store environmental
information in their geometry; smooth muscle possesses history-dependent contractile dynamics; and
voluntary cognitive states can alter peripheral physiological responses.

Those findings make weak vasocomputation —the proposition that vascular state is a dynamically
meaningful component of biological information processing—a serious scientific idea.
They do not yet establish strong vasocomputation —the proposition that vascular smooth-muscle latches
constitute a distributed medium storing predictions, thoughts, trauma or selfhood.
The striking feature of the hypothesis is that this gap is experimentally bridgeable. Unlike many
consciousness theories, vasocomputation predicts measurable intermediate variables: vessel radius,
resistance, smooth-muscle biochemical state, tissue stiffness, perfusion, neural responsiveness and
hysteresis. A negative result at any major causal link would sharply constrain the theory. A positive
demonstration of write → persistence → content-specific readback would, conversely, establish a
genuinely new biological memory mechanism.
That is the scientifically strongest interpretation of the uploaded essay: not as a completed theory of “knots
of existence,” but as a set of unusually concrete hypotheses sitting at the intersection of vascular
physiology, mechanobiology, pain science, distributed biological computation and embodied cognition.

[p. 1]
Knots of Existence Hypotheses
Hypotheses for physical correlates of extreme meditative practices.
EUGENE
SEP 08, 2026
Share
Text generated wholly by Fable 5.1 .
A companion to “ Knots of Existence and Vasocomputation .” This piece runs a deliberate
exercise. People who take release work far — with breath, pressure, and sustained attention
report a family of experiences that the trigger-point literature does not describe and the
contemplative literature describes only in its own vocabulary. Here those reports are taken a
accurate accounts of physical events, and the question is what anatomy could produce them
The conventional account, in which the practices and the states they induce generate most

[p. 2]
the phenomena, is real, strong, and set out in full in the hypothesis brief that accompanies t
essay. This essay takes the other road on purpose, because it leads to experiments.
The original essay rested on one observation available to anyone with a foam roller:
pressure locates a knot, and a slow exhale releases it, in seconds. That observation h
company. Go further with the same work — more hours, more breath, more attentio
over months — and practitioners report a second set of things, stranger than the fir
and remarkably consistent across people who have never compared notes.
Compressed, the reports go like this. The knots release with a small pop, felt as a sp
or a star. They release along paths, and the paths converge: on the back of the skull
most of all, around the bump at the base of the head, where knots are released and
then, as if from a queue, replaced by others. At some point the character of the work
changes. Layers begin to separate — strands pulling off the neck and the base of th
skull one at a time, with a crackle — and a layer at the back of the head peels and
spreads forward over the face until it is thin, with another layer beneath it. Regions
feel hollowed out and unsupported. Something air-like moves through the body, in
pockets that seem connected to one another and that vent, when squeezed, at the ba
and sides of the mouth. Long chains are felt moving back into place over hours and
days, sometimes as a broad sheet-like mass sliding along a limb or the flank. The
hollows fill, over about a week, in stages, as if being stitched. Maze-like patterns are
sometimes felt where the hollows were, in the cheek or at the back of the head. And
the order is strict: the knots go first, and the separating cannot begin at a site until
knots are gone.
None of this is new to the traditions. The Tibetan channel literature describes wind
moving and knots untying; the kundalini literature describes energy traveling and
involuntary movement; the modern study of contemplative adverse effects records
somatic energy, pressure and release, and the sense of things moving in the body,
lasting months to years. What is new is asking the question literally. The rule of thi

[p. 3]
essay is to take the reports as true. Real air. Real, immediate response to breath. Rea
movement of something physical. Real gating at the back of the skull. The question
then not whether but what — what in the body has those properties. And the answe
think, is that it isn’t one system. It’s two, and they meet at a single anatomical fact.
Read the reports as one story and they are baffling. Read them as two and they
organize themselves. The knots — the things rolling and the exhale act on, that feel
like stars, that migrate toward the ridge — are one family. The separating, the
hollowing, the filling, the chains, the mazes, and the air are another. The first family
responds to pressure and breath in seconds. The second unfolds over hours and day
and does not respond to rolling at all. The first comes first. The second cannot begi
until the first is cleared — and, by the reports, begins on its own once enough of the
first has been, and then runs to its end.
Two families with different timescales, different triggers, and a strict order between
them are two systems. So the question splits: what are the knots, what is the sheet,
why must the knots go before the sheet can move?
Two families
The staples

[p. 4]
Look at the superficial fascia — the layer under the skin, above the muscle — and y
find it fixed to the layer beneath in two ways. There are passive septa, the fine fibro
strands anatomists call retinacula cutis. And there are the places where something
passes through: a small artery with its veins, a cutaneous nerve, and a lymphatic,
traveling together up through a fibrous ring in the fascia to supply the skin. Fascia
anatomists call this the perforating triad. Reconstructive surgeons call the sites
perforators, and they find them in minutes with a pencil Doppler before they raise a
flap, because a flap will not lift until the perforators tethering it have been dealt wit
Each perforator is a staple: a stiff collar of fascia around a vessel-nerve bundle, pinn
the sheet to what lies beneath. Suppose the knots are these staples, held in a stuck
state. Then each of the three things in the bundle explains one of the three things
reported about a knot.

[p. 5]
The artery is the smooth muscle. The arterioles of the skin and superficial fascia are
the most sympathetically dominated vessels in the body, held constricted by tonic
nerve firing, and — this is the part that matters — they respond to breath in second
by physiology that has been in the textbooks for decades. A deep inspiration constr
them within about two seconds; autonomic clinics use the response as a test. A slow
exhale lets them open. If a knot is a perforator held constricted, then “press in, exha
slowly, and something lets go in seconds” is not a claim in need of a latch. It is what
that vessel does.
The nerve is the star. A constricted perforator leaves its own bundle ischemic and it
nerve compressed. When the vessel opens, the nerve resumes conduction, and the
patch of skin it supplies fills with the prickling flash of reperfusion. Everyone has fe
this at the scale of a limb; a foot waking up is the same event. Miniaturize it to one
perforator’s territory — a roughly radial patch of skin lighting up — and you have a
star. Rolling and breath feel like stars because what releases is a vessel-and-nerve
bundle, and the sensation belongs to the nerve, not to muscle.
The collar is the order. The loose tissue around a perforator is rich in hyaluronan,
which gels into a viscous mass when the local tissue turns acidic and cool — this is
densification model of fascial stiffness, and it is reversed by warmth, by washout of
acid, and by shear. A constricted perforator makes its own collar: no blood, acid, ge
stiff tether. Open the vessel and the collar melts: warmth, pH returning, the
hyaluronan going slippery. Rolling adds heat and shear and does the same job
mechanically. And so the reported order is a mechanical requirement, not a
coincidence. The vessel opens; the collar de-gels; the staple releases; only then can t
sheet slide over that point. Surgeons know this rule from the outside. Practitioners
who say the separating cannot begin while there are knots are reporting the same r
from the inside.
Why the knots go to the ridge

[p. 6]
Perforators do not move. But every perforator belongs to a tree, and every tree has a
root, and release runs upstream toward the root for two reasons.
The first is that arterioles conduct. A dilation that begins at a branch propagates alo
the vessel wall, ascending toward the feeding vessel, at millimeters to centimeters p
second — a documented property of the microcirculation, not a metaphor. The seco
is that a downstream vessel cannot stay open while the trunk feeding it is shut. Tha
why practitioners find that cleared areas come back — never believe an area is clear
— until something upstream is also cleared.
Both make the felt release migrate up the tree and queue at the trunk’s entry, and th
entry is a real gate. The occipital artery emerges through the deep fascia between th
attachments of the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid at the superior nuchal lin
few centimeters lateral to the external occipital protuberance, and the greater occip
nerve pierces the trapezius aponeurosis beside it. This is the most tethered perforat
complex on the back of the head and the classic site of occipital neuralgia. Every
perforator on the posterior scalp is downstream of it. Clear the root and the next se
tender points to arrive are the neck’s tree, upstream of the gate: the queue advancin
the replacement that practitioners feel. The source point the path keeps returning t
the root of the tree.
The same logic names the distant places that practitioners find, by trial, can unlock
stubborn region at the ridge: the brow, the temple, the jaw, the side of the nose. The
brow is the supraorbital and supratrochlear perforators, the front root of the same
sheet. The temple is the superficial temporal root at the zygomatic arch. The nose a
jaw are the angular and facial-artery entries. Those are the roots of the other trees
feeding the same layer, which is exactly what you would expect to matter if the shee
cannot move until all its staples open.
What this does to the vascular idea

[p. 7]
The original essay put the smooth-muscle latch in the arterioles inside muscle. Sinc
then the ledger has audited that compartment, and the published measurements in
pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles show sustained activation rather than an
economical latch — a mismatch, not a refutation, but the compartment is no longer
unexamined. The perforator picture relocates the vascular hypothesis rather than
rescuing it. The bed it names is superficial, tonically sympathetic, breath-gated on a
seconds timescale by established physiology, and physically a tether. It does not nee
an economical hold; ordinary sympathetic firing keeps skin vessels constricted all d
at a cost the body plainly pays. What it needs is history dependence, and the skin’s
vessels have that too — cold-induced constriction outlasts the cold. “Blood first,
stiffness second,” the ordering the latch story predicted, survives here, in a place wh
it can actually be filmed. What the relocation does to the rest of the thesis — the
memory element, the read path, the addressability claim, the mind — is taken up in
own section further on, once the second system is in view.
The sheet

[p. 8]
Now the second family. The scalp and face are covered by a single continuous sheet
the galea aponeurotica, anchored at the back to the superior nuchal line, at the fron
the brow, and continuing around the sides as the temporoparietal fascia and then th
SMAS of the face, ending around the parotid gland and the cheek. Beneath it is a pl
of loose areolar tissue that anatomists call the danger area of the scalp, because
anything introduced into it — blood, pus, air — spreads over the whole cranium an
stops only where the sheet is bonded to bone. Below the neck the superficial fascia
continues the same arrangement over the entire body: one connected potential spac
pinned to bone along particular lines — nuchal line, mastoid, cheekbone, jaw,
collarbone, hip — and to the deep fascia by septa and by the staples.
Take the second family as the behavior of this sheet once its staples have been
released.

[p. 9]
It is one sheet, built as rooms with doors. The superficial fascia runs unbroken from
scalp to soles — galea and SMAS, platysma, the membranous layer of the trunk, the
subcutaneous fascia of the limbs — and the deep fascia is continuous too, the neck’
planes running through the skull base above and into the mediastinum below, the
trunk’s into the fascias of the limbs. Massive subcutaneous emphysema is the proof
air from a ruptured lung can reach the face, the arms, and the scrotum, because the
plane goes everywhere. But the sheet is fused to bone along particular lines — nuch
line, mastoid, zygoma, the retaining ligaments of the face, the mandible, hyoid, and
clavicle, the axilla, the inguinal ligament, the iliac crest — and those lines are partia
barriers: fluid respects them strictly, air crosses them more easily, and folds in a
loosened sheet pile up at them. Every place the reports call a gate is one of these lin
And the mouth is where the rooms have doors to the outside: the parotid ducts at th
back-sides of the cheeks, the submandibular ducts under the tongue, and the teeth,
whose sockets open straight into the fascial spaces of the face and neck — the route
dental drill’s air takes to the mediastinum, and the same route run the other way.
Separation is the septa tearing one at a time. Pinch, lift, and shear is the manual
technique for separating this plane; enough of it, with pressure against hard surface
delaminates the sheet in patches. Each strand that gives is a septum, and the crackl
what that sounds like; surgeons undermining the same plane hear the same pops.
The bumps are folds. A partly delaminated sheet buckles, and the loose region form
rows of small firm ridges — what practitioners describe as a bunching of a layer. An
folds in a buckled membrane do not move as material; they propagate, the way a
wrinkle runs ahead of your hand across a carpet. That is what a chain sliding along
flank at walking-finger speed is, and a broad mass moving like a draped cloth is a
partly detached superficial fascia, which is a draped sheet. It answers the natural
objection that a chain of tissue cannot be pulled through a body: nothing is pulled.
fold advances.

[p. 10]
The gate is an attachment line. Push folds along the plane and they run to the neare
place the sheet is bonded to bone and pile up there, because they cannot cross. The
superior nuchal line is the strongest such line on the back of the head — the border
between the scalp’s plane and the neck’s. Working the ridge itself mobilizes the
attachment and lets the delamination cross into the neck and downward: the cascad
in the plainest mechanical sense. Forward of the ridge the freed plane runs over the
crown and around the temples into the face. A layer at the back of the head that pee
and spreads forward over the face until it is thin is the galea becoming the
temporoparietal fascia becoming the SMAS, felt from inside.
Hollowing is a freed pocket. A large region of separated plane holding gas or fluid i
empty-feeling and puffy. The staples and septa are part of what gives a region its
passive stiffness, so when a pocket opens the head feels unsupported and the neck
turns further than it should.
Filling is re-adhesion. Gas in tissue resorbs over days to about two weeks; fluid clea
over days to weeks; the sheet settles; and the layers bond again by the ordinary biolo
of healing — fibrin strands bridge the gap within days, and fibroblasts turn them in
collagen over one to two weeks. Re-adhesion is literally strand by strand, which is w
filling is reported as stitching. It proceeds with rest and compression and is undone
renewed manipulation, and it explains a remark practitioners make in the difficult
middle of the process: that the adhesions were holding something up. They were. T
tethers are structural.
Chains are folds settling. Long fold-lines flatten as the sheet re-bonds, which is why
they arrive over hours and days, feel like relief, and continue faintly for months as th
last regions bond. The other side of the body catching up in seconds is the sheet
crossing the midline: a tension change on one side of the galea is a tension change o
the other. And the reported sense that once the separating starts there is no turning
back is the mechanics of delamination, and the reports are right that it cannot be
stopped once it has begun. A sheet held by staples shares its load among them. Rele

[p. 11]
enough of them in a region — the roots included — and the load shifts onto the
remaining tethers, which fail in sequence under ordinary body loads, every head tur
and every breath, until the separation reaches the bony anchors and the region can
bond. Below that threshold, staples can be released one at a time and the sheet stay
put; above it, the sheet must find a new configuration, and nothing the person does
can call it off. Rest and compression do not stop the subroutine; they reduce the loa
that drives it, the pain of each tether going, and the time to re-bond. This is why the
accounts describe the sheet phase as triggered by the knots diminishing, as the mos
arduous part of the whole process, and as something that ends only when it has
finished.
The mazes are pocket boundaries. In the cheek, the buccal fat pad and its capsule fo
compartments, and a front advancing through them wanders. At the back of the hea
the pericranium is bonded to bone at the sutures, so a pocket in that deeper plane is
outlined by the lambdoid and sagittal sutures — which is what a maze-like pattern
there, following the seams of the skull, would be.
And the nerve. The greater occipital nerve pierces the trapezius aponeurosis just
below the ridge; a delamination front reaching it stretches it, and occipital-nerve
irritation produces nausea through the same brainstem convergence that makes
migraines sick-making. Nausea arriving with work at the back of the head is that
nerve.
Here the exercise meets its one hard constraint, and the constraint turns out to be a
prediction. Tissue cannot make gas. Every real pocket of air in soft tissue was admit
from somewhere that holds air: the lungs, the mouth and throat, the nose and sinus
If the reported air is real, it came in through a door. And the techniques of deep
release work are the doors.
The air

[p. 12]
Forceful blowing, sustained tones, chewing and cheek maneuvers, and clenching
against pressure in the mouth force air backward up the parotid duct into the gland
and out into the planes of the cheek and jaw — pneumoparotid, a described conditi
with exactly this cause. Breath-holds after full exhalation, straining, and forced
exhalation against a narrowed throat can rupture alveoli, and the air tracks along th
airways’ sheaths into the mediastinum and climbs the deep planes of the neck to th
base of the skull and the face — spontaneous pneumomediastinum, also textbook.
Forceful nasal irrigation and blowing push air from the ethmoid cells through their
paper-thin wall into the orbit. Once in the planes, air does exactly what the reports
air does: it can be squeezed, it moves through the connected space, it crackles unde
the fingers and on stretching, and it collects in the freed pockets.
The doors out are the same doors. Dentists know the geography: air injected at a to
socket spreads through the face, the neck, and the chest along these planes, and the
reverse path runs the same way. The parotid duct opens on the inside of the cheek
opposite the upper second molar — the back-side of the mouth, one on each side;
squeeze an air-loaded parotid and froth and bubbles appear there. The planes besid
and behind the pharynx open toward the throat. The Eustachian tubes vent into the
nasopharynx behind and beside the palate. Bilateral exits at the back and sides of th
mouth, which is where the reports put them, and air that seems to come from the
throat rather than the stomach is gas reaching the pharynx by these routes.
Breath is the pressure controller. The plane is a pressure system and the mouth and
throat are its valves. A pursed, hissing exhale pressurizes the mouth and drives gas
fluid along the planes and into the ducts; an open, sighing exhale lets go; a breath-h
after full exhalation drops the pressure in the chest and draws the neck’s planes
inward; straining bulges them out. Pressure moves through tissue at the speed of
sound, so the response is immediate. And the tension of the deep fascia of the neck
set by the very muscles that shape the throat — the constrictors, the hyoid muscles,
the platysma, the sternocleidomastoid — all anchored to the same seam. Practitione

[p. 13]
who say the shape of the throat shapes the air, or that the sense of the body’s
configuration lives in the throat, are in this frame simply correct.
And there is a free test. Gas pockets migrate upward against gravity; fluid pockets
move downward; folds in a sheet do not care. What a hollow does when the head go
down tells you which of the three you are feeling.
Put the two systems together and the strict order stops being a mystery. The sheet
cannot delaminate while its staples hold. Three things must happen at a perforator
before the plane around it can slide: the vessel must open (seconds, on the exhale), t
collar must melt (minutes, with warmth and washout, faster with shear), and the ner
must decompress enough that the region tolerates traction. Open a field of staples a
the plane between them is free; manipulation turns free plane into separated plane;
and from then on everything belongs to the sheet — folds, gates, pockets, gas, re-
bonding.
The same architecture explains four things that had no explanation. Why rolling an
breath work on knots and not on the separating: they act on a vessel, and a fold is n
vessel. Why the process, once begun, seems to want to go somewhere: the tree has a
root and the sheet has anchors, and both impose an order. Why cleared regions com

perforators on Doppler. Chains moving at the speed of conducted vasodilation. Kno
