with all its perforators and none of its knots.
What the literature already supports

[p. 30]
Before the experiments, the audit. None of the studies below was designed to test th
picture, and none tests the two claims that are new here — that the point is a
perforator and that the state travels the tree. Read together, though, they show that
every other link in the chain has been observed somewhere, and that the chain is m
of ordinary physiology rather than new biology.
The state at a knot has been imaged, in muscle. Sikdar and colleagues put gray-scal
ultrasound, vibration sonoelastography, and Doppler on trigger points in the upper
trapezius and found discrete hypoechoic nodules, stiffer than the surrounding tissu
with abnormal flow around them ( Sikdar et al. 2009 ). Shah’s microdialysis had alread
found the acidic, mediator-rich milieu of local ischemia at active points, and Hubba
and Berkoff’s needle a millimeter-scale electrical nidus. Release brings blood: with
microdialysis catheter inside an active trigger point, ischemic compression produce
transient rise in local blood flow ( Moraska et al. 2013 ), and a single dry-needling
stimulus in the trapezius raised blood flow and oxygen saturation at the needled sit
for fifteen minutes without changing distant sites ( Cagnie et al. 2012 ) — in healthy
volunteers, so a needle effect rather than a knot effect, but a local reperfusion all th
same. The writer is real: mental arithmetic raised the electrical activity at a trigger
point while the adjacent muscle stayed silent ( McNulty et al. 1994 ), and in the rabbi
model the same spontaneous activity is reduced by the alpha-blocker phentolamine
tying it to sympathetic drive ( reviewed here ). Arendt-Nielsen’s group has also repor
an attenuated skin blood-flow response over latent trigger points, the first hint of a
cutaneous vasomotor abnormality at a knot. What no one has measured is which ve
is throttled, or the order in which vessel, stiffness, and nerve change at a release.
The bed the perforator model names behaves as claimed. A deep inspiratory gasp
produces a reflex sympathetic constriction of skin arterioles within a couple of
seconds, relaxing on the exhale — a standard autonomic test with decades of literat
and a recent review ( 2026 ), measured most often in the finger, where arteriovenous
anastomoses are dense; its briskness in the hairy skin of the neck and scalp is less
studied. A continuous-wave Doppler on the radial artery detects the same reflex,

[p. 31]
which is why the cheap version of the release experiment is plausible ( Journal of
Neurology, 2004 ). And the superficial fascia is richly innervated, with about a third
its nerve fibers autonomic and concentrated around its vessels ( Fede et al. 2022 ).
The collar has a literature. Stecco’s group described the hyaluronan-rich loose
connective tissue between fascial layers and proposed that its densification is the
substrate of myofascial pain ( Stecco et al. 2011 ), then showed by ultrasound that the
loose-connective-tissue sublayers of the neck fascia are thicker in chronic neck pain
and thin with treatment ( Stecco et al. 2014 ). Langevin’s group found about twenty
percent less shear glide between thoracolumbar fascia layers in chronic low back pa
( Langevin et al. 2011 ), a result a 2026 systematic review places among a set of fascial
thickness, echogenicity, and shear-strain differences in chronic back pain ( Europea
Spine Journal, 2026 ). Hydrodissection — separating a nerve from the fascia around i
with fluid — relieves entrapment syndromes across the body, which is the collar mo
in clinical use ( systematic review ).
Stuck perforators are already a diagnosis. Anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment,
cluneal entrapment, occipital neuralgia, and meralgia paresthetica are discrete tend
points where a neurovascular bundle crosses a fascial ring, and one 2025 case is the
whole model in a paragraph: Carnett’s sign at the tender point, a pulsating perforat
artery on color Doppler directly beneath it, and resolution when the nerve was
hydrodissected at its penetration site ( Yoshinaga et al. 2025 ). Whether the
identification generalizes to ordinary knots is the untested part, and the acupunctu
literature has been circling it for forty years. Heine reported that most classical poin
sit at perforations of the superficial fascia by a vessel–nerve bundle ( Heine 1988 );
Langevin and Yandow found eighty percent of points on connective-tissue planes
( 2002 ); Dorsher’s comparison of the trigger-point manual with the acupoint atlas fou
above ninety percent anatomic correspondence and referred-pain patterns that follo
meridians ( Dorsher 2009 ); a thermographic pilot found perforating vessels at acupo
( Álvarez-Prats et al. 2019 ), and a 2024 dissection of the five-shu points of the arm
concluded that perforating cutaneous vessels are a key feature of acupoints ( Meng e

[p. 32]
al. 2024 ). Against this, a multicentre dissection that found the meridians tracking
fascia found vessel–nerve bundles at only a few points ( Maurer et al. 2019 ), which is
why a blinded coincidence study, not another dissection, is what settles it.
The tree behaves as claimed. That a dilation started at one point on an arteriole
propagates along its wall, upstream to the feeding vessel, independently of flow, wa
shown by Segal and Duling ( Science 1986 ), and the electrical basis of that conductio
is now a mature field with a recent Physiological Reviews treatment ( 2025 ). Upstrea
dependence among knots has a clinical demonstration: Hong and Simons found tha
inactivating a key trigger point inactivated its satellites without treating them ( 1993
And the count is consistent with the ladder: Taylor and Palmer’s map of the body’s
major cutaneous perforators — an average of 374 of half a millimeter or more,
reinforced by numerous smaller indirect vessels — is its top rung ( 1987 ).
The sheet, the air, and the gate are documented mechanisms. Self-induced
pneumoparotid from habitual Valsalva behaviors has produced cervicofacial
emphysema tracking into the mediastinum ( 2025 ); pediatric cases show the air bubb
in the parotid and the deep cervical spaces on ultrasound and CT ( 2025 ); and air from
dental drill reaches the retropharynx and mediastinum through the same planes
( review ). The myodural bridge, described in 1995, is now a “complex” of fibers from
three suboccipital muscles and the nuchal ligament to the dura, conserved across
vertebrates, with a proposed role in cerebrospinal fluid circulation ( 2026 review ).
The phenomenology is documented outside this essay. The largest study of
meditation-related experiences found that the most common somatic report was
pressure or tension that built and then released, with release associated with positiv
affect, surges of energy, sometimes electricity-like currents through the body, and
involuntary movements ( Lindahl et al. 2017 ). And the intramuscular family is not a
human peculiarity: equine trigger points show the same spontaneous electrical acti
as human and rabbit ones ( Macgregor & von Schweinitz 2006 ), and a 2026 review
argues them as a primary cause of lameness ( Frontiers in Veterinary Science ).

[p. 33]
What remains is exactly the two links the essay adds. No one has tested whether
ordinary tender points sit on perforators, and no one has watched a release with tim
resolution in any tissue, so the order of events — vessel, stiffness, nerve — is
unknown, and every model in this essay makes a different prediction about it. Thos
two experiments are the ones that turn the list above into one chain or break it.
Several experiments fall straight out of this picture, and none of them is expensive.
Map the staples. Blinded palpation marks the tender points on a region of scalp, ne
back, or hip; a second blinded operator maps the perforators on the same region wi
pencil Doppler, the way it is done before a flap; a third computes coincidence again
What would show it

[p. 34]
chance. If knots are stuck perforators, the tender points sit on the perforators, and t
most tender sit on the largest trunks at their fascial exits. If they don’t, this picture
wrong, and we will know in an afternoon.
A word on instruments, because Johnson’s essay says, rightly, that seeing a release
requires ultrasound. It does. To watch stiffness and perfusion change together at on
site, time-locked to the exhale, you need an imaging modality — shear-wave
elastography for the stiffness and a sensitive Doppler mode for the flow, or at the
surface, laser speckle for perfusion and a high-frequency probe for structure. A pen
Doppler can do none of that; it is an 8 MHz continuous-wave probe that turns the fl
under its tip into a sound, with no image, no stiffness, and no anatomy. But the
question it answers is the prior one — are the tender points where the perforators a
— and for that it is the right instrument rather than a compromise: locating
perforators by ear is what surgeons do with it, it costs a few hundred dollars, and a
region takes minutes, which is what lets the coincidence study run across many peo
in a day. What changed is not the instrument but the depth of the target. Johnson’s
latched arteriole lay a centimeter deep in muscle, where only ultrasound reaches; a
perforator is a few millimeters down, in the pencil Doppler’s range. Its limits shape
the design — it hears flow, not structure, favors larger perforators (which biases
toward a null), and is occluded by probe pressure, so mapping must be done at fixed
light pressure by a blinded operator who is not the one marking the tender points. T
layered version is: pencil Doppler for the map; on the hits, high-frequency ultrasoun
with power Doppler and elastography to see the vessel pierce the fascia and the coll
around it; and for the release itself, a non-contact method at the surface. There is al
a cheap intermediate: a recording continuous-wave Doppler held over a mapped
perforator during a breath release. If the flow signal jumps on the exhale, that is
“blood first” for the price of a vascular Doppler.
Film a star. The original keystone experiment — image a single release with
elastography and Doppler — had to reach into muscle. The perforator bed is at the
surface, where laser speckle contrast imaging resolves skin blood flow at millisecon

[p. 35]
rates with no depth problem. Put the field over the occiput or the upper trapezius,
mark a knot and a sham site, record breath and carbon dioxide and a button press a
each felt release, apply calibrated pressure. If the knot is a perforator, there is a loca
flash of perfusion time-locked to the exhale and to the star, absent at the sham site,
and absent when the pressure is applied during an inhale-and-hold — because the
inspiratory reflex should block it. If the sparks are hyperventilation, the perfusion
changes are global, equal at sham sites, and track carbon dioxide rather than the
button.
Free a collar without breath. Under ultrasound, a perforator can be hydrodissected
a few milliliters of saline placed around the bundle at its fascial ring, the technique
already used for entrapped nerves. If a knot is a collared perforator, hydrodissection
the perforator should release it in seconds with no breath and no pressure, and the
should arrive with the fluid; if a knot is motor guarding, saline around a vessel does
nothing. This is the cleanest single test of the identification, and a clinic that does
nerve hydrodissection could run it in a week.
Time the chains. Have practitioners who feel releases travel mark the path and rate
the speed, and measure skin perfusion along the path with laser speckle or laser
Doppler. Conducted vasodilation ascends at millimeters to centimeters per second,
and the Chinese propagated-sensation literature reports about the same; a traveling
perfusion wave under a traveling sensation, blocked by pressing on the line or cooli
it, would tie the physiology, the reports, and the tradition together. A sensation that
travels with no perfusion wave beneath it is a percept.
Lay the curves on top of each other. The knot census the case already proposes —
palpation, algometry, and elastography at fixed sites across the age span — can add
laser-Doppler measure of cutaneous microvascular reactivity at the same sites at no
real cost. The perforator model predicts knot burden rises as cutaneous reactivity fa
site by site, and that children, whose perforators are open, are nearly clean.

[p. 36]
Image the seam. The myodural bridge is visible on MRI and increasingly on
ultrasound, and the suboccipital muscles can be measured. For practitioners who
report the base-of-skull release, imaging of the atlanto-occipital interval before and
after — suboccipital muscle thickness and texture, dural displacement with head
flexion, cervical flexion-rotation range — would show whether a release there is a
measurable change at the master tether. It would not show what awakening is. It
would show whether it has a somatic address.
And, for anyone in the middle of the second family, the ordinary tools of an emerge
department settle the sheet and the air directly. Point-of-care ultrasound shows gas
tissue as bright foci with a characteristic dirty shadow and shows a separated plane
a dark strip of fluid between fascial layers. Crepitus under a flat hand is the bedside
sign. Massage of the parotid produces froth at its duct if the duct has been insufflat
A photograph across a hollow-to-fill cycle shows the swelling. The gravity test cost
nothing.
If the model is right, a machine that dissolves knots is not exotic. Almost every
component already exists as a medical or cosmetic device; what nobody has done is
assemble them in the right order at the right rate. The order and the rate are the
invention. The hardware is off the shelf.
Start with what a knot needs, per the model. The arteriole has to open; the hyaluron
collar has to de-gel; the tether has to be freed; the nerve has to quiet. Each has a too
Heat opens the cutaneous bed more completely than anything else the body does —
thermoregulatory vasodilation in a sauna or a hot immersion is the largest vasomot
response there is — and slow breathing or a sympathetic block does the same on
command. Heat and shear de-gel hyaluronan, and so does hyaluronidase, an injecta
enzyme already used to dissolve hyaluronan fillers under the skin. Ultrasound-guid
hydrodissection frees a bundle from its ring, and radial shockwave delivers shear at
Could you build a machine?

[p. 37]
depth. A local anesthetic quiets the nerve. Seen this way, shockwave therapy for
trigger points, trigger-point injections, and dry needling at a perforator are knot
machines that already work without knowing why, and the sauna is a whole-body
perforator-opener that stops working the moment you step out, because the collar a
the tether and the writer are still in place.
The sheet needs something different, and the first design decision is to refuse what
the reports describe. Peeling was what happened when people kept going past the
staples; it is an injury with weeks of instability. What a sheet needs for glide is not
separation but de-gelling of the loose plane — heat, movement, shear, enzyme at th
persistent collars. If a region genuinely needs separating, that exists too, and it is
surgery: the tumescent technique floods the subcutaneous plane with liters of dilute
saline and hydrostatically lifts the sheet over large areas, subcision devices cut the
septa, and liposuction surgeons then manage the re-bonding with compression
garments, which is the filling phase engineered. A knot-free body may not need any
it.
The machine, then, is a sequence more than a device.
Map. Doppler and high-frequency ultrasound with elastography: where the perforat
are, which are tender, which are stiff. You cannot treat a tree you have not drawn, an
the map is also the measurement that tells you whether anything is working.
Roots first. Release the trunks at their fascial exits — occipital, supraorbital, tempo
the cluneal nerves at the hip, the motor points around the shoulder blade — by
hydrodissection or shockwave, because nothing downstream stays open while the
trunk is shut. This is the step every practitioner discovers by trial, and the step the
machine would take by design.
Descend the tree, exhale-gated. Warm the region, then deliver shear pulses timed to
end-exhalation from a respiration sensor, since the inspiratory reflex closes the bed

[p. 38]
and a pulse landing on an inhale is wasted or worse. Re-map after each session. Tre
what is still stuck; leave what has opened alone.
Glide, not peel. De-gel the loose plane with heat and movement between sessions, a
enzyme where a collar will not soften.
Consolidate. Compression and rest between sessions, so that re-bonding keeps pace
with release. This is the safety mechanism, and it is the whole difference between a
treatment and a cascade. A sheet shares its load among its staples; once enough are
open in a region, the rest fail in sequence and the region must delaminate to its
anchors and re-bond before it is stable again — the phase the reports describe as
unstoppable once triggered, and the worst part. The machine’s job is to stay below t
threshold: release staples no faster than the plane re-bonds around them, so the she
is never asked to find a new configuration all at once. Whether the endpoint can be
reached that way — knot-free without ever triggering the sheet phase — is untested
the reports describe only the fast route, through it. The slow route is what the
traditions’ pacing would amount to, if it works.
Retrain the writer. None of it holds if the nervous system keeps writing to the same
addresses. A body reset to a young knot burden, under the same stress and posture
breathing, refills on the timescale of stress rather than of aging. Slow-breathing and
heart-rate-variability training are the cheapest part of the machine and the part
without which the rest decays.
What such a machine could not safely do is the thing the question asks about:
everything at once. A device that cleared every staple in a day would produce a body
without support, pockets that fill and re-bond as scar, and whatever comes with
releasing every held territory at the same time — the reports and the meditation
adverse-effects literature describe that without needing the anatomy. The useful
machine does a few percent a week, with a map before and after. And that is roughl
what breath, heat, pressure, and attention already do when they are done slowly, wh
is the traditions’ actual technology. Their pacing was not caution for its own sake. O

[p. 39]
this model it was rate-matching release to re-bonding, and the machine’s first
specification is to do the same.
Everything in this essay that admits air into the body, separates a plane, or stretche
nerve is an injury, and the practices that would do it are documented hazards. Force
blowing, sustained pressure in the mouth, breath-holds and straining, and aggressiv
irrigation of the nose are the recognized causes of pneumoparotid, cervicofacial
emphysema, and orbital emphysema. Hyperventilation with breath-holds produces
hypocapnia, altered states, and fainting, and combined with cold water it has killed
people. Hours of forceful manipulation injure skin and nerves and, with dehydratio
or fasting, can break down muscle. Water loading produces dangerous drops in bloo
sodium. Sleep and food deprivation produce despair. The contemplative traditions
preserved a warning about untying too fast, and the modern literature on the advers
effects of intensive practice says the same thing in clinical language: destabilization
that can last months or years. Nothing here is a protocol. Anyone inside a process li
the second family needs an ordinary medical assessment — electrolytes, creatine
kinase, hydration, sleep — and a reduction of intensity. Not because that stops the
sheet phase: on this model, and by the accounts, once it is triggered it runs to its
anchors and then re-bonds, and it ends only when it has finished. But because rest,
compression, hydration, sleep, and someone watching are what make that phase
survivable and shorten the re-bonding, while pushing through it with more release
does the opposite. The sense that it cannot be stopped is correct. The inference tha
more release is the way out is not.
I said at the start that this essay takes one road on purpose. The other is the one a
physician would take first, and it is not a strawman. Hyperventilation produces exac
the sparks called stars. A muscle inhibited by pain feels detached and recovers with
A caution that is also part of the mechanism
The other road

[p. 40]
rest. Air drawn into the throat by suction maneuvers and expelled — supragastric
belching — is a known behavior that worsens under attention. Sleep loss and fastin
distort the body’s map of itself until parts seem to have gone missing. And anything
that relocates in the blink of an eye is a percept, not a tissue. The brief lays all of tha
out at full strength.
The two roads do not disagree about everything. Both say the tender points are real
and change within a session — state, not scar. Both say any real air was let in by the
practices. Where they part is precise and testable: whether the stars are local events
perforators or distributed events organized by attention; whether there are separate
planes with gas in them or swelling and a distorted map; and whether the knots mu
clear before the separating for a mechanical reason or because technique escalates —
the first predicts that the sheet phase begins at a threshold of cleared knots whatev
the technique, the second that it tracks the technique. The Doppler map, the laser
speckle field, and one ultrasound decide between them.
So the exercise ends where the original essay did, with a measurement nobody has
made. But the measurement has moved. It is at the surface now, at the places where
small artery and a nerve come up through the fascia together, a few centimeters to t
side of the bump at the back of the skull. Someone should put a Doppler pen there a
press.

evidence.title: Spontaneous EMG activity confined to the trigger-point nidus
evidence.sourceStatement: Monopolar needle EMG recorded simultaneously from trapezius trigger points and adjacent non-tender fibers found sustained spontaneous activity in the 1–2 mm nidus of all trigger points and none in the non-tender sites; amplitude was higher in tension-headache and fibromyalgia patients than in normals. The authors hypothesized sympathetically activated intrafusal (spindle) contractions.
evidence.editorInference: Whatever a knot is, it is electrically maintained: a discrete island of ongoing activity in muscle that is nominally at rest — state, not scar.
limitations: 1993, small sample, one lab; the signal's generator is still contested (endplate potentials vs spindles).
The recorded activity is skeletal-muscle electrophysiology; nothing here measures vasculature.

origin.ref: Knots of Existence essay §two experiments; verified 2026-08-22

evidence.title: Mental arithmetic selectively raises trigger-point activity
evidence.sourceStatement: With needle electrodes in trapezius trigger points and adjacent control sites, a psychological stressor (mental arithmetic) increased EMG activity at the trigger points while control sites in the same muscle remained comparatively quiet, without generalized muscle tensing.
evidence.editorInference: A purely mental event, involving no movement, turned up the signal inside one tender point and not a centimeter away: the write half of any storage account, caught in motion.
limitations: n=14, 1994, same lineage as Hubbard & Berkoff — the two EMG studies are one line of evidence.

The essay's follow-up claims (relaxation training lowering activity; phentolamine infusion quieting the site) come from the same lineage and were not independently verified in this project — no primary citation located.
No vascular endpoint was measured; sympathetic drive to spindles or endplates fits the data without any vascular storage.

origin.ref: Knots of Existence essay §two experiments; verified 2026-08-22

evidence.title: The latch-bridge model: force maintained after activation falls
evidence.sourceStatement: A minimum kinetic model of smooth-muscle cross-bridge interaction in which dephosphorylated but still-attached cross-bridges ("latch bridges") detach only slowly, reproducing the experimental observation of high sustained stress at low levels of myosin phosphorylation — economical force maintenance after activation subsides.
evidence.editorInference: Biology ships a cheap, history-dependent hold: the mechanism the featured hypothesis needs exists and is textbook physiology. Whether it is engaged at tender points is a separate, untested question.
limitations: Established in vascular/visceral smooth-muscle preparations over minutes-to-hours timescales; indefinite in-vivo holds at addressable sites are an extrapolation.
Molecular interpretation still under refinement (regulated phosphatase activity, cooperativity).

evidence.title: The hemo-neural hypothesis as proposed
evidence.sourceStatement: Moore and Cao propose that hemodynamics — blood flow and volume — may actively modulate neuronal information processing rather than merely supplying metabolic support, through candidate mechanical, thermal, and chemical pathways, and predict consequences for sensory gating and disease.
evidence.editorInference: The read path of the loop, stated as a hypothesis in 2008: this paper defines the claim rather than demonstrating it. The essay's "Rosalind Cao" should be Rosa Cao.
limitations: A hypothesis paper: proposes mechanisms, presents no new experimental demonstration.

evidence.title: Blood-pressure pulsations modulate neurons via mechanosensitive channels
evidence.sourceStatement: Physiological blood-pressure pulsations were shown to modulate central neuronal activity through mechanosensitive ion channels in rat preparations and awake animals, on rapid timescales.
evidence.editorInference: Direct causal evidence for the vascular-mechanical-to-neural direction the hemo-neural hypothesis requires — sixteen years after it was proposed, the read path has a demonstrated mechanism.
limitations: Rat brain, not human periphery; demonstrates instantaneous mechanosensation, not storage or content-specific readout.

origin.ref: Stored Tension critical report §neurovascular signaling; verified 2026-08-22

evidence.title: Acidic, mediator-rich biochemical milieu at active trigger points
evidence.sourceStatement: Microdialysis-style sampling found biochemicals associated with pain and inflammation — including bradykinin, substance P, and CGRP, in a more acidic milieu — elevated at active myofascial trigger points, in sites both near to and remote from the points, relative to comparison conditions.
evidence.editorInference: Something is there and it is chemically angry — exactly the milieu chronic local ischemia would produce, though guarding-induced compression would produce it too. Note the title's own qualifier: the elevation was not purely local.
limitations: Small study (the critical report's audit gives nine volunteers); localization vs systemic effects hard to separate.

origin.ref: Knots of Existence essay §Shah microdialysis; verified 2026-08-22

evidence.title: Imaging systematic review: trigger points are quantifiably distinct
evidence.sourceStatement: Per the critical report's audit of this systematic review (33 studies): biomechanical and blood-flow imaging parameters can distinguish active and latent trigger points from healthy tissue, with the review emphasizing the need for better reproducibility and diagnostic-accuracy research.
evidence.editorInference: The imaging literature's positive residue — including the Doppler flow abnormalities the essay reads as the latch's footprint — survives systematic review, with reproducibility caveats attached. This record's characterization is second-hand from the critical report; the review's full text has not been checked.
limitations: Heterogeneous techniques and trigger-point definitions across the included studies.
Characterization taken from the critical report; not verified against the paper's full text.

evidence.title: Attention regulates acute inflammation (histamine skin prick)
evidence.sourceStatement: In preregistered within-subject experiments (57 volunteers), directing attention toward the sensations of a standardized histamine skin prick produced ~1.5-fold smaller and faster-resolving wheal and flare responses than distraction, in ~90% of participants across two cohorts. Skin conductance, heart rate, skin temperature, and self-reported anxiety did not differ between conditions, while heart-rate variability was higher under internal attention; a sensory route (degraded by lidocaine) and a top-down vagal route (surviving lidocaine) both contributed.
evidence.editorInference: A controlled existence proof of the channel the synthesis needs: voluntary interoceptive attention, with no arousal change, measurably regulating peripheral physiology at a specific site. The measured tissue was a vascular bed — but the demonstrated route is vagal immune regulation over ~20 minutes, not seconds-scale latch release.
limitations: Single lab, published 2026-08-17; acute model in healthy skin; molecular mediators not directly measured (authors' own caution).
The authors note the parasympathetic system does not innervate skin directly; nothing here concerns trigger points or smooth-muscle latches.

origin.ref: Knots of Existence essay §attention study; verified against the NHB paper 2026-08-22

evidence.title: Slow breathing's documented autonomic correlates
evidence.sourceStatement: A systematic review of slow-breathing studies in healthy humans found reproducible increases in respiratory sinus arrhythmia and heart-rate variability and related autonomic and central nervous system changes, consistent with a shift toward parasympathetic dominance.
evidence.editorInference: The breath is a real autonomic lever — the one voluntary handle on the system. This establishes the global shift only; the local, site-specific unlatching the featured hypothesis adds on top is exactly what has never been measured.
limitations: Global cardiovascular indices in healthy subjects; no local tissue or tender-point measurements.

origin.ref: Stored Tension critical report §does exhalation release knots; verified 2026-08-22

evidence.title: The Quintner–Bove–Cohen critique of the trigger-point construct
evidence.sourceStatement: The authors argue the myofascial trigger-point construct rests on circular reasoning and unproven assumptions: the lesion has never been demonstrated, examiner reliability is poor, and the clinical phenomena attributed to trigger points can be better explained by other mechanisms (they propose neurogenic inflammation of peripheral nerves).
evidence.editorInference: The serious peer-reviewed case against the entire observational base of this case's featured hypothesis. Its force against the latch reading is partial: the critique targets the classic taut-band construct and its diagnosis, not the existence of tenderness or of the instrumented abnormalities — and a vascular mechanism is, if anything, closer to the critics' "it isn't the muscle" instinct than the classic theory is.
limitations: Answered point-by-point by Dommerholt & Gerwin (2015); the debate remains open rather than settled in the critics' favor.

origin.ref: Stored Tension critical report §trigger-point audit; verified 2026-08-22

evidence.title: Systematic review: trigger-point palpation is not reliably reproducible
evidence.sourceStatement: A systematic review of examination-reliability studies concluded that manual physical examination for myofascial trigger points has not been demonstrated to be reliable or valid, in part because no accepted reference standard exists, and could not currently be recommended as an objective diagnostic test.
evidence.editorInference: The measurement problem underneath everything: studies on both sides of this case locate their object by palpation. Any decisive experiment must first solve blinded, instrumented localization — which is why the keystone study design requires it.
limitations: Assesses the manual exam, not instrumented detection; imaging-anchored localization may escape the problem.

evidence.title: Johnson's three vasocomputation hypotheses
evidence.sourceStatement: Johnson proposes three hypotheses: Compressive Vasomotion (vasomotion functions as a compression sweep collapsing ambiguous neural patterns), Vascular Clamp (vascular contractions freeze local neural patterns for their duration, functioning as predictions and medium-term memory), and Latched Hyperprior (contractions held long enough engage the smooth- muscle latch-bridge, durably freezing nearby circuitry until the corresponding prediction resolves) — mapping the stack onto Buddhist tanha.
evidence.editorInference: The synthesis this case examines, stated by its originator. It is a self-published theoretical program: as of August 2026 its experimental projects (per Edge City materials cited in the critical report) seek direct evidence rather than reporting it.
limitations: Not peer reviewed; no experimental validation published; the mapping from latch physiology to cognitive content is the theory's central unproven step.

origin.ref: opentheory.net essay; verified against the live page 2026-08-22

evidence.title: First-person report: the two-key release protocol
evidence.sourceStatement: The essay reports, as first-person and practitioner experience: pressure locates a knot but does not release it; release comes with breath — press into a knot, breathe slowly, and on a long exhale something lets go, in seconds. Fresh knots yield in a session; old ones take months.
evidence.editorInference: The anchor phenomenon of the whole case, honestly labeled: first-person phenomenology from the hypothesis's proponent (in an essay whose text was AI-generated at the author's direction), consistent with widespread practitioner lore, measured by no one.
limitations: Testimony, not measurement; proponent source; expectation and attention effects cannot be excluded from any first-person release report.

evidence.title: Tender-point ubiquity and the missing census
evidence.sourceStatement: The essay reports that anyone with a foam roller can locate dozens of tender points, densest around hips and shoulders and more numerous with age; it cites fibromyalgia-era community tender-point exams (medians of 6 in women and 3 in men, counts tracking distress) as the closest existing data — and observes that no knot census (count, distribution, or age curve) has ever been performed.
evidence.editorInference: The community-exam figures are the essay's second-hand characterization — the underlying rheumatology survey has not been located and verified in this project. The census gap itself is confirmed by the critical report and is the case's cheapest decisive research opportunity.
limitations: Second-hand statistics; underlying citation unverified — figures should not carry weight until traced.

evidence.sourceStatement: The report's graded evidence matrix assigns grade D — no direct evidence located — to both linchpin propositions: "a knot releases objectively in seconds during exhalation" (no synchronized time-resolved imaging study found) and "the releasing element is vascular smooth muscle" (no study identifies a smooth-muscle latch at a trigger point; the EMG chatter is neuromuscular, not vascular).

evidence.title: Hysteresis is not yet memory: the missing write–store–read demonstration
evidence.sourceStatement: The report argues that biological memory requires state that depends on prior input, can later be read out, and discriminates between different prior inputs — criteria the latch literature does not address. It notes that the closest empirical precedent is not mammalian: Physarum slime mold demonstrably stores nutrient locations in the tube-diameter hierarchy of its living flow network (Kramar & Alim 2021), a genuine write–store–read loop — in an organism whose tubes are its own motile body.
evidence.editorInference: A thermostat's hysteresis is not autobiographical memory. The weak form of vasocomputation (vascular state shapes neural computation) is now plausible; the strong form (latches store thoughts) has no direct evidence, and the best evidence that flow networks can store information comes from an organism very unlike us.
limitations: The Kramar & Alim citation was reproduced from the report and its PNAS identifier not independently re-verified; used here as the report's argument, not as an imported source.

evidence.title: A whole-body ultrasound platform exists — as a prototype, for composition
evidence.sourceStatement: Butterfly Network confirmed Midjourney Medical's June 2026 announcement of a full-body tomographic ultrasound scanner: a prototype ring of 40 Ultrasound-on-Chip modules scanning a submerged body in about sixty seconds, body-composition imaging as the announced application, spa deployment planned for 2027, and no diagnostic clearance.
evidence.editorInference: Relevant to feasibility of the knot census, not to any mechanism claim: the coverage problem that made whole-body tissue mapping impractical is being attacked commercially. The essay's "just a firmware update" gloss overstates it — volumetric elastography and microvascular Doppler on this hardware are undemonstrated engineering, per the critical report.
limitations: Prototype announcement with commercial incentives; images composition (structure), not the stiffness/flow state channels a census needs; unverified performance claims; no clearance.

evidence.title: Study table: energetic cost has never been measured in any arteriole, so the economy argument rests entirely on conduit arteries
evidence.sourceStatement: Across sixteen rows spanning 1981-2022, contemporaneous energetic measurement — oxygen consumption, lactate release, or ATP turnover — appears only in large tonic arterial preparations (swine and porcine carotid, at zero transmural pressure), and in no arteriole or resistance microvessel of any bed. No located study satisfies all four conditions the study set: skeletal-muscle arteriole or smaller, physiological temperature and transmural pressure, maintained force or diameter, and a contemporaneous energetic or cycling measurement. The frozen literal queries aimed at microvascular energetics returned nothing, as did two further searches run specifically for arteriole-level oxygen consumption and ATP economy.
evidence.editorInference: The energetic feasibility step under VASO-C020 — that a knot can be held cheaply — is an extrapolation across both vessel class and caliber, not a borrowed-and-demonstrated mechanism. The extrapolation may still be correct; what the ledger can now say is that nobody has measured it where the hypothesis needs it, and that this is a gap in the literature rather than a gap in this case's reading of it.
evidence.exactLocator: Study VASO-S001, finding 1 (full table on the study page)
limitations: Absence of a demonstration is not a demonstration of absence; the study's own limitations record that discovery ran against PubMed, Europe PMC and Crossref, which cover the older non-indexed energetics literature poorly.

origin.extractedBy: Aletheia editorial AI (Claude Opus 5, Cursor cloud agent)

evidence.title: Study table: in pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles, maintained constriction tracks maintained activation rather than the latch signature
evidence.sourceStatement: Three rows are pressurized skeletal-muscle resistance vessels — rat cremaster and gracilis — in which LC20 phosphorylation was measured against diameter. In all three, maintained constriction is accompanied by maintained or rising phosphorylation rather than by force held while activation falls: 27.7% at 30 mmHg rising to 39.6% at 120 mmHg (Zou, Ratz & Hill 1995, at 34 degrees C in roughly 100-micrometre arterioles); a monophasic rise correlated with instantaneous wall tension (Zou, Ratz & Hill 2000); and 40% already at 10 mmHg rising to about 55% at 80 mmHg with no further change to 140 mmHg (Moreno-Dominguez et al. 2013, which attributes the sustained constriction to Rho-kinase-mediated Ca2+ sensitization and actin polymerization). The 2000 paper states that spontaneous arteriolar tone "represents a state of maintained smooth muscle activation that requires increases in [Ca2+]i and myosin light-chain phosphorylation."
evidence.editorInference: This is the first record in the case bearing directly on the tissue compartment VASO-C020 names, and it does not fit the latch picture: at arteriole caliber the published measurements show sustained activation, not an economical dephosphorylated hold. It is a mismatch rather than a refutation — none of the three studies was designed as a latch test, all held their stimulus present throughout, and none measured energetic cost. What it removes is the assumption that the arteriole compartment is simply unexamined; it has been examined with the right molecular readout, and what was found there points at a different mechanism for holding constriction.
evidence.exactLocator: Study VASO-S001, finding 2 (full table on the study page)
limitations: All three rows were built from published abstracts; full texts were not accessible, so temperature is recorded for only one of the three and endothelial status for none.
Myogenic tone is by construction a response to a maintained stimulus, so these studies could not have shown input-free persistence even if it exists.

origin.extractedBy: Aletheia editorial AI (Claude Opus 5, Cursor cloud agent)

evidence.title: Study table: latch behaviour is not generic across vascular smooth muscle, and the divergence was never followed downstream
evidence.sourceStatement: Paired rows from rabbit femoral and saphenous artery record sustained isometric stress at falling intracellular calcium in the femoral (1.3e5 N/m2 at 10 min, MLC phosphorylation 42%) against a 40% stress loss in its own muscular branch (0.8e5 N/m2, phosphorylation 28%), which the authors attribute to expressed motor proteins that do not support latch-bridge formation, together with greater MLC phosphatase. The pressurized follow-up reports the same asymmetry in diameter behaviour. Forward citation chaining from both 2006 papers located no study extending the comparison into arterioles or the microcirculation.
evidence.editorInference: VASO-C010 states a capability, and the capability is real — but the ledger should no longer be read as saying that vascular smooth muscle generically latches. The one published comparison between a vessel and its own downstream branch found the behaviour present in the parent and absent one branch order later, which makes vessel type and motor-protein phenotype load-bearing variables rather than incidental ones. That nobody has run the comparison further down is the specific gap VASO-R004's paired-caliber design now exists to close.
evidence.exactLocator: Study VASO-S001, finding 3 (full table on the study page)
limitations: One publication and one laboratory supply both arms of the comparison; the femoral/saphenous divergence has not been independently replicated, and the study records the two 2006 papers as non-independent.
The saphenous artery is a named conduit artery, not a resistance microvessel, so it constrains how far downstream the finding can be read.

evidence.title: Ballyns 2011: arteries near active trigger points show higher pulsatility and more frequent retrograde diastolic flow — but 31% of palpably normal sites show it too
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that on colour Doppler prominent vessels were seen close to trigger points and that "vessels near active sites had a significantly higher pulsatility index" (median 8.3) than normal sites (median 3.0, P < .05). It states that in 27 of 49 active sites (55%) "retrograde diastolic flow was observed compared to 21 (40%) and 15 (31%)" for latent and normal sites, with the occurrence significantly higher in active and latent than normal sites (P < .01).
evidence.editorInference: This is the primary behind the 'abnormal local hemodynamics' the ledger previously held only via the Mazza review. It supports VASO-C005 as a measurable blood-flow difference, but the difference is graded: nearly a third of palpably normal sites in these patients show the same waveform, so the signature is a gradient across symptomatic muscle, not a marker. The interrogated vessels are pulsatile arteries or enlarged arterioles typically >1 mm, within 1–2 cm of the point, not the microvessels the latch attribution names.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC3493620 author manuscript, Results, paragraph beginning 'On color Doppler imaging' (via open-access PMC copy)
limitations: Within-patient 'normal' sites in symptomatic patients; no pain-free control group.
Pulsatility index was not a good classifier of site type because of large variance, per the source's ROC analysis.
Vessel caliber (>1 mm, 1–2 cm from the point) is far from the arteriolar compartment VASO-C020 requires.

evidence.title: Ballyns 2011: resistivity index did not differ between active, latent and normal sites
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that "No differences in RI values were detected between normal", latent and active sites, and that "the PI was not a good classifier of active, latent, or normal sites because of the large variance."
evidence.editorInference: A negative result recorded in its own right: one of the two Doppler indices shows no difference, and the other does not classify sites. The vascular signature at trigger points is partial, not categorical.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC3493620 author manuscript, Results, paragraph beginning 'On color Doppler imaging' (via open-access PMC copy)
limitations: Within-patient comparison in symptomatic subjects; the authors attribute the similarity partly to proximity of normal sites to trigger points.

evidence.title: Ballyns 2011: the Doppler indices do not cleanly separate sites
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that "No differences in RI values were detected between normal", latent and active sites, and that the pulsatility index "was not a good classifier of active, latent, or normal sites" because of large variance; it adds that blood-flow measures "did not perform well as classifiers of the site type".
evidence.editorInference: Narrows VASO-C005: blood flow differs on one index at group level but does not distinguish individual sites, and a second index shows no difference. The claim's 'measurably differ' survives in the weak group-level sense only.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC3493620 author manuscript, Results (Doppler paragraph) and Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Although most trigger points are located' (via open-access PMC copy)
limitations: Same subjects and sites as VASO-E025; not an independent observation.

evidence.title: Ballyns 2011: no pain-free control group; 'normal' sites sit in symptomatic muscle
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states as a limitation that "our study did not include a control group of pain-free patients", that pain-free sites were instead marked at least 5 cm from latent and active sites, and that because all patients had at least one palpable trigger point the observed blood-flow characteristics "do not represent the normal variation".
evidence.editorInference: Every comparison in this source is within symptomatic patients. The 31% retrograde-flow figure at 'normal' sites may therefore be either a true baseline rate or spillover from neighbouring points; the source itself cannot say which. This caps the strength of VASO-E025 and VASO-E026.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC3493620 author manuscript, Discussion, paragraphs beginning 'We suspect the large variance' and 'Although we believe that measuring' (via open-access PMC copy)
limitations: Author-stated limitation; no external data on pain-free variation was shown.

evidence.title: Ballyns 2011: high-resistance flow near trigger points is compatible with compression by contracture, inflammation, or transducer pressure as much as with distal constriction
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports that arteries near active and latent sites had highly pulsatile flow with retrograde diastolic flow more often than normal tissue, and that "prominent blood vessels were observed in the close vicinity of trigger points". It offers two explanations for pulsatile flow — increased compliance/volume of the vascular compartment, or increased outflow resistance — and lists possible causes of the latter: "muscle contracture at the trigger point that compresses the capillary/venous bed", anatomic geometry of the trapezius apex, local vasoconstriction due to inflammation, or externally applied pressure from the transducer. It frames its integrated-hypothesis discussion around capillary constriction, ischemia and hypoxia and notes increased vessel presence as a possible angiogenic response.
evidence.editorInference: Recorded as supporting because increased downstream resistance near trigger points is what VASO-C020's 'chronic local ischemia' predicts — but at effectively zero diagnosticity: the source itself names skeletal-muscle contracture compressing the bed (the conventional account) as a candidate cause and does not mention smooth-muscle latch. Nothing here separates arteriolar smooth muscle from mechanical compression, and the vessels observed are conduit-scale, not microvascular.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC3493620 author manuscript, Results (Doppler paragraph) and Discussion, paragraphs beginning 'The integrated trigger point hypothesis' and 'In this study, results from the Doppler waveforms' (via open-access PMC copy)
limitations: Vessels interrogated were pulsatile arteries or enlarged arterioles typically >1 mm, 1–2 cm from the point.
Alternative mechanical explanations are given equal standing by the authors.
No perfusion measurement in the muscle bed itself; Doppler waveform only.

Second reader (claude-sonnet-5, 2026-09-09) disputes the stated direction: The quotes and paraphrases accurately reflect the Doppler paragraph and Discussion text, including the equal-standing alternative explanations for pulsatile flow. However, labeling this 'supports' VASO-C020 is questionable: the source explicitly treats compression by contracture, inflammation, or transducer artifact as equally plausible alternatives to a latch-bridge vascular-autonomic mechanism, so the passage more properly qualifies or contextualizes the claim rather than affirmatively supporting it—this is registered as dissent rather than grounds for rejection. All other elements (quote fidelity, statement scope, locator accuracy, independence, relevance to the claim) check out.

evidence.title: Ballyns 2011: palpation is the reference standard and remains subjective
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that although most trigger points are located and classified from history and physical examination, "results can vary depending on the clinician’s training and experience", and that the visual analog scale, pressure-pain threshold and palpation are the reference standards "but they are still subjective measures".
evidence.editorInference: A proponent group conceding the point the critics press: the reference standard is examiner-dependent. Weak because it is an assertion in a discussion section rather than a reliability measurement; the ledger already holds the systematic review (VASO-E011).

evidence.title: Ballyns 2011 pilot: trigger-point area and pulsatility index fell over follow-up visits after dry needling in three active cases
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports a pilot of three active cases and one latent case imaged at later time points after dry needling: "The trigger point area and PI decreased for all 3 active cases" with time and increased slightly for the latent case; the authors state there were too few cases to draw conclusions.
evidence.editorInference: Background only for VASO-C011: an imaged change in stiffness and Doppler indices after an intervention, but over visits, not seconds, and after needling, not pressure or breath. It shows the measures move; it does not bear on the seconds-scale timescale argument.
evidence.exactLocator: PMC3493620 author manuscript, Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Data for a pilot study including 3 active cases' and Figure 7 caption (via open-access PMC copy)
limitations: n = 3 active cases, uncontrolled, author-flagged as too few for conclusions.
Timescale of visits, not of a release event.

evidence.title: Simons, Hong & Simons 2002: endplate noise is characteristic of, but not restricted to, trigger points
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports a needle examination at one test site and two control sites in 11 muscles of 10 subjects, with the endplate zone determined electrically: "Endplate noise without spikes occurred in all 11 muscles at trigger-point sites", "in four muscles at endplate zone sites outside of trigger points" (P = 0.024), and "did not occur in taut band sites outside of an endplate zone" (P = 0.000034). It concludes that endplate noise seems to be "characteristic of, but is not restricted to, the region" of a trigger point.
evidence.editorInference: This qualifies VASO-C002's 'confined to a nidus, absent in adjacent non-tender muscle': spontaneous activity was found at 4 of 11 non-tender endplate-zone sites. Hubbard–Berkoff's silent control sites may have lain off the endplate zone rather than demonstrating exclusivity. The correct comparator for the nidus is a matched endplate-zone site, which neither Hubbard–Berkoff 1993 nor McNulty 1994 used, as far as the ledger records. The prevalence gradient (11/11 vs 4/11 vs 0/11) still supports 'more common at trigger points'.
evidence.exactLocator: Abstract, Results and Conclusion, Am J Phys Med Rehabil 81(3):212–222, via the Ovid landing page at doi:10.1097/00002060-200203000-00010
limitations: Abstract only; per-site amplitudes and subject details not shown.
Design described by the source as nonrandomized and unblinded; 10 subjects.
Authors are proponents of the trigger-point construct.

evidence.title: Simons, Hong & Simons 2002: prevalence of endplate noise at trigger-point, endplate-zone and off-zone taut-band sites
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that endplate noise occurred at all 11 trigger-point sites, "in four muscles at endplate zone sites outside of trigger points", and "did not occur in taut band sites outside of an endplate zone"; it describes the study as "This nonrandomized, unblinded needle examination of myofascial trigger points".
evidence.editorInference: Direct anchor for the two observation claims: endplate noise occurs outside trigger points when the site is in the endplate zone, and not in taut bands off the zone. Together they imply the electrical signature tracks the endplate zone first and the trigger point second, which is the conventional skeletal-endplate reading.
evidence.exactLocator: Abstract, Design and Results, via the Ovid landing page at doi:10.1097/00002060-200203000-00010

Second reader (claude-sonnet-5, 2026-09-09) disputes the stated direction: The quoted passage on p.4 matches the source text verbatim and is fairly summarized as the essay's own restatement of needle-EMG findings, correctly located. However, VASO-C003 specifically claims selective activation at trigger points versus quiet adjacent control sites in the same muscle, and the p.4 passage only states that trigger-point chatter rises with stress and falls with relaxation without any mention of a control site remaining quiet (that detail appears only later, on p.5, describing the McNulty study). Using this general, control-free statement to 'support' a claim whose core content is about site-selectivity is a stretch; it is better characterized as background context for the claim rather than direct support, so I dissent on the direction while agreeing the record is otherwise accurately sourced and relevant.
